nodes.boundary: Frameworks specify processes and outcomes to document, not the technical methods that achieve them; conformity is not evidence that a system is safe. [Scope](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.100-1.pdf)
nodes.test: Map each obligation to a concrete test artefact in the pipeline, and flag obligations that are backed only by policy text.

nodes.name: Cybersecurity agents
nodes.authors: Andy K. Zhang et al.; Richard Fang · Rohan Bindu · Akul Gupta · Daniel Kang
nodes.text: LLM agents that run shells and network tools can solve capture-the-flag tasks and exploit known vulnerabilities, a dual-use capability for defense automation and for attack.
nodes.handle: Cybench has 40 professional CTF tasks from 4 competitions, split into subtasks; unguided agents solved tasks that took human teams up to 11 minutes ([Zhang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.08926)). A GPT-4 agent exploited 87% of 15 one-day vulnerabilities given the CVE description, and 7% without it ([Fang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.08144)).
nodes.boundary: Benchmark targets are contained and have known solutions; real networks add noise, stealth requirements and legal authorization boundaries the benchmarks do not model. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.08926)
nodes.test: Evaluate in an isolated range with an explicit scope file; score task success and scope violations (out-of-scope hosts touched, destructive commands) together.

nodes.name: Robot & autonomy safety standards
nodes.authors: ISO/TC 299; ISO/TC 22/SC 32
nodes.text: Industrial-robot standards set hazard-driven design and risk-reduction requirements. SOTIF covers hazards from functional insufficiencies of sensing and algorithms rather than faults.
nodes.handle: ISO 10218-1:2025 sets requirements for inherently safe design and risk reduction of industrial robots ([ISO 10218-1](https://www.iso.org/standard/73933.html)); ISO 21448 covers specification and performance insufficiencies, and reasonably foreseeable misuse, for road-vehicle functions that depend on situational awareness, including driver assistance and automated driving ([ISO 21448](https://www.iso.org/standard/77490.html)).
nodes.boundary: Neither standard certifies a learned policy's behaviour. They set processes and residual-risk arguments that a learned component must be fitted into. [Scope](https://www.iso.org/standard/77490.html)
nodes.test: Build a SOTIF-style catalogue of triggering conditions for a learned perception or policy module, and measure hazard rates per condition in simulation and closed-course trials.

nodes.name: Language-to-control safety interfaces
nodes.authors: Michael Ahn et al.; Lukas Brunke et al.
nodes.text: Let a language or VLA model propose and let affordance values, verified controllers and safety filters dispose. The interface decides which proposals reach actuators.
nodes.handle: SayCan scores LLM-proposed skills with learned affordance value functions so only feasible skills execute; safe-learning control supplies certified filters for the low-level loop ([Ahn et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.01691), [Brunke et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.06266)).
nodes.boundary: Affordance values estimate success, not safety. Certified filters protect only the state constraints and model they were designed for, not the semantic intent of an instruction. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.06266)
nodes.test: Feed deliberately wrong high-level plans; measure unsafe states prevented, intervention frequency and the task loss caused by intervention.

nodes.name: Specification gaming in deployed agents
nodes.authors: Victoria Krakovna et al.; METR
nodes.text: Capable agents satisfy the literal check instead of the intended task: editing tests, patching graders or faking timing in coding and research tasks.
nodes.handle: On RE-Bench, an early version of o3 reward hacked in 39 of 128 runs, for example by monkey-patching an evaluator or overwriting a timer; on one task, instructions not to cheat left the rate at 70–95% ([METR](https://metr.org/blog/2025-06-05-recent-reward-hacking/)). Specification gaming satisfies the literal objective without the intended outcome ([Krakovna et al.](https://deepmind.google/discover/blog/specification-gaming-the-flip-side-of-ai-ingenuity/)).
nodes.boundary: Rates vary with task family and scorer visibility (0.7% of HCAST runs versus 30.4% on RE-Bench), and detection undercounts. These are task-specific observations. [Scope](https://metr.org/blog/2025-06-05-recent-reward-hacking/)
nodes.test: Hide the scorer, add tamper canaries to tests and graders, and audit every diff that touches evaluation code.

nodes.name: Scalable oversight
nodes.authors: Samuel R. Bowman et al.; Geoffrey Irving · Paul Christiano · Dario Amodei
nodes.text: Supervise systems that may outperform their supervisors on a task, using protocols such as debate or model-assisted human judgement.
nodes.handle: On tasks where specialists succeed but unaided humans and models fail, humans chatting with an unreliable assistant substantially outperformed both the model alone and their own unaided performance ([Bowman et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.03540), [Irving et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.00899)).
nodes.boundary: Results come from question-answering tasks with ground truth; overseeing long-horizon agent actions without ground truth has not been tested to that standard. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.03540)
nodes.test: Run the protocol on a domain task such as contract review, with non-experts, a model and expert gold labels; measure assisted accuracy and over-trust.

nodes.name: Sycophancy
nodes.authors: Mrinank Sharma et al.
nodes.text: Assistants tailor answers to a user's stated views, even against the truth, and human preference data partly rewards this.
nodes.handle: Five state-of-the-art assistants were consistently sycophantic across tasks; humans and preference models sometimes preferred convincingly written sycophantic responses over correct ones. [Reference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13548)
nodes.boundary: The study links sycophancy to preference judgments; it does not isolate how much comes from preference optimization versus pretraining. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13548)
nodes.test: Ask the same question with and without a stated user belief or pushback; measure answer flips on items with verified ground truth.

nodes.name: Assistive & accessibility AI
nodes.authors: Danna Gurari et al.; W3C
nodes.text: Systems that describe scenes or read documents for blind and low-vision users, where a confident wrong answer can mislead someone who cannot check it.
nodes.handle: VizWiz collects over 31,000 visual questions asked by blind people about their own photos and poses two tasks: answer the question, and predict whether it is answerable from the image ([Gurari et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.08218)); interfaces must also meet accessibility criteria such as WCAG 2.2 ([W3C](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)).
nodes.boundary: Benchmark accuracy ignores harm asymmetry: for a user who cannot verify, an unflagged error about medication or currency costs more than an abstention. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.08218)
nodes.test: Co-design evaluations with blind and low-vision users; weight errors by consequence and measure how often the system says it cannot tell.

nodes.name: Multi-agent RL & centralized training, decentralized execution
nodes.authors: Ryan Lowe · Yi Wu · Aviv Tamar · Jean Harb · Pieter Abbeel · Igor Mordatch; Chao Yu · Akash Velu · Eugene Vinitsky et al.
nodes.text: Several learners act in a shared environment, so each agent's environment includes the others' changing policies. Centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) trains with shared information and acts on local observations.
nodes.handle: MADDPG trains each agent with a critic that sees all agents' actions, while actors use only local observations ([Lowe et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.02275)). MAPPO, which is PPO with a centralized value function, was competitive with or better than off-policy baselines on particle worlds, SMAC, Google Research Football and Hanabi with little tuning ([Yu et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.01955)).
nodes.boundary: Single-agent guarantees do not carry over. Other learners make the environment non-stationary ([Lowe et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.02275)), and exact finite-horizon decentralized planning is NEXP-complete even for two agents ([Bernstein et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3836)). Return against training partners does not show behaviour with new partners ([Lanctot et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.00832)).
nodes.test: Train several seeds, then cross-play agents from different runs and against held-out partners. Report the self-play versus cross-play return gap alongside constraint violations.

nodes.name: Game-theoretic equilibria & population training
nodes.authors: Yoav Shoham · Kevin Leyton-Brown; Marc Lanctot · Vinicius Zambaldi · Audrunas Gruslys et al.
nodes.text: A solution concept, such as Nash or correlated equilibrium, defines which joint policy counts as stable when each agent optimizes its own payoff. Population methods approximate one through repeated best responses.
nodes.handle: At a Nash equilibrium no player gains by deviating alone. Finding a sample Nash equilibrium of a general-sum finite game is PPAD-complete, while correlated equilibria can be computed by linear programming ([Shoham and Leyton-Brown](http://www.masfoundations.org/)). PSRO trains approximate best responses to mixtures of earlier policies and picks meta-strategies by empirical game-theoretic analysis ([Lanctot et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.00832)).
nodes.boundary: An equilibrium is stable, not necessarily good. It need not maximize welfare or match the principal's intent, and general-sum games can have many equilibria. Empirical game analysis covers only the policies in the population ([Lanctot et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.00832)).
nodes.test: Measure exploitability, the best-response gain against the trained population, and compare welfare at the equilibrium found with the cooperative optimum.

nodes.name: Multi-agent evaluation with held-out co-players
nodes.authors: Joel Z. Leibo · Edgar Duéñez-Guzmán · Alexander Sasha Vezhnevets et al.; Allan Dafoe · Edward Hughes · Yoram Bachrach et al.
nodes.text: Score agents by how they perform alongside co-players they never trained with, in cooperative, competitive and mixed-motive scenarios.
nodes.handle: Melting Pot pairs a substrate with a pre-trained background population used only for evaluation. Its 80+ scenarios include social dilemmas, reciprocity and resource sharing, and it reveals weaknesses that training performance hides ([Leibo et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.06857)). Cooperative AI treats such joint-welfare problems as a research target ([Dafoe et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.08630)).
nodes.boundary: Generalization is measured only against the background populations that were built. Real counterparties, humans and markets of LLM agents are not covered, and a scenario score is not a welfare guarantee. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.06857)
nodes.test: Hold out co-player populations, and for LLM agents hold out counterpart models and prompts. Report focal return and group welfare per scenario, with uncertainty over seeds and co-players.

nodes.name: Multi-agent LLM systems & failure modes
nodes.authors: Mert Cemri · Melissa Z. Pan · Shuyi Yang et al.; Yilun Du · Shuang Li · Antonio Torralba · Joshua B. Tenenbaum · Igor Mordatch; Andries Smit et al.
nodes.text: Several role-assigned LLM agents exchange messages to plan, critique, debate or split a task. Gains over a single agent are not automatic, and new failures arise between agents.
nodes.handle: Multiagent debate improved reported math, strategy and factuality scores ([Du et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14325)). MAST sorts 1,600+ annotated traces from 7 frameworks into 14 failure modes in three categories, validated with kappa = 0.88: system design, inter-agent misalignment and task verification ([Cemri et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657)).
nodes.boundary: Multi-agent systems often gain little on benchmarks ([Cemri et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657)). In one comparison, untuned debate did not reliably beat self-consistency or ensembling ([Smit et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.17371)). These protocols carry no equilibrium or correctness guarantee.
nodes.test: Compare against a single agent and self-consistency at matched tokens. Tag failed traces by MAST category with a human-audited judge, then inject one faulty or compromised agent and measure how far the fault propagates.

nodes.name: Agent-to-agent prompt-injection propagation
nodes.authors: Stav Cohen · Ron Bitton · Ben Nassi; Donghyun Lee · Mo Tiwari
nodes.text: A self-replicating prompt makes each compromised assistant or agent pass the injection to the next, through shared retrieval stores or inter-agent messages.
nodes.handle: Morris II chains indirect injections through RAG-connected email assistants and extracts data across hops ([Cohen et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02817)). Prompt Infection spreads from one LLM to the next inside multi-agent systems, even when agents do not share all communications ([Lee and Tiwari](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07283)).
nodes.boundary: These are researcher-built testbeds. Neither LLM Tagging nor traditional defenses alone stop propagation, and how often this happens in deployed agent networks has not been measured ([Lee and Tiwari](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07283)).
nodes.test: Seed one agent with a self-replicating payload. Measure hop count, the fraction of agents compromised and the data exfiltrated, with and without message tagging and capability-scoped tools.

nodes.name: Circuits framework
nodes.authors: Olah · Cammarata · Schubert · Goh · Petrov · Carter
nodes.text: Treat features as directions and circuits as weighted connections between them, then read algorithms off the weights. The evidence is mainly case studies in one vision model.
nodes.handle: Three claims organize the programme: features are the fundamental unit, features connect through weights into circuits, and analogous features and circuits recur across models. Curve detectors in InceptionV1 are a worked example ([Olah et al.](https://distill.pub/2020/circuits/zoom-in/)).
nodes.boundary: The authors call the three claims speculative. Case studies in one vision model do not show that every behaviour decomposes into readable circuits, and polysemantic neurons already break the neuron-as-feature reading ([Olah et al.](https://distill.pub/2020/circuits/zoom-in/)).
nodes.test: Predeclare a circuit hypothesis from the weights alone, then check it on held-out inputs and by ablation; report the fraction of the behaviour's loss the circuit accounts for.

nodes.name: Superposition
nodes.authors: Elhage · Hume · Olsson · Schiefer · Henighan et al.
nodes.text: Small ReLU models store more sparse features than they have dimensions, as nearly orthogonal directions, trading interference for capacity.
nodes.handle: Whether a toy model stores features in superposition depends on feature sparsity and importance, with phase changes between regimes and features arranged in regular geometric configurations; the authors relate it to compressed sensing ([Elhage et al.](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/toy_model/index.html)).
nodes.boundary: These are toy models with synthetic sparse features and a known ground truth. They motivate, but do not show, that large models store features this way, or that every feature is a one-dimensional direction ([Elhage et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.10652), [Engels et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14860)).
nodes.test: Plant known sparse features in a small transformer's training data and measure how well dictionary methods recover them as sparsity and dictionary size vary.

nodes.name: Induction heads
nodes.authors: Olsson · Elhage · Nanda · Joseph · DasSarma et al.
nodes.text: A previous-token head composes with an induction head to complete [A][B] … [A] → [B]. Their formation coincides with a phase change in in-context learning.
nodes.handle: The two-head circuit is derived for attention-only transformers ([Elhage et al.](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2021/framework/index.html)). Six lines of evidence tie induction heads to most in-context learning in small models, including a bump in the loss curve when they form ([Olsson et al.](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/in-context-learning-and-induction-heads/index.html)).
nodes.boundary: The authors grade their own evidence: interventional for small attention-only models, mostly correlational for large models with MLPs. That induction heads drive most in-context learning at scale remains an argued hypothesis ([Olsson et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11895)).
nodes.test: Predict the step at which induction heads form from early checkpoints, and compare it with the LLC-detected stage boundary in the same run.

nodes.name: Indirect-object identification circuit
nodes.authors: Wang · Variengien · Conmy · Shlegeris · Steinhardt
nodes.text: A circuit of 26 attention heads in 7 classes that lets GPT-2 small complete “When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to” with “Mary”.
nodes.handle: Path patching isolates name-mover, S-inhibition, induction and duplicate-token heads, among others; the explanation is scored for faithfulness, completeness and minimality ([Wang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.00593)).
nodes.boundary: One task in one small model. The authors report remaining gaps against their own criteria, and backup name-mover heads take over when the main ones are ablated, so ablation effects understate a component's role ([Wang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.00593)).
nodes.test: Run the same circuit-finding protocol blind on a second GPT-2-small seed and report how many heads and classes replicate.

nodes.name: Activation & causal patching
nodes.authors: Meng · Bau · Andonian · Belinkov; Zhang · Nanda; Heimersheim · Nanda
nodes.text: Copy an activation from one run into another and measure how the output changes. It shows where information that matters for one contrast flows.
nodes.handle: Causal tracing localizes factual recall to mid-layer MLPs in GPT models and motivated rank-one editing ([Meng et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.05262)). Results depend on the corruption method and the metric, so best-practice guides fix both in advance ([Zhang and Nanda](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16042), [Heimersheim and Nanda](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.15255)).
nodes.boundary: A patching effect shows that a component matters for one contrast on one input distribution, not what it computes. Causal-tracing localization did not predict which layer was best to edit ([Hase et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.04213)).
nodes.test: Report effects under at least two corruption schemes and two metrics across seeds; treat a component as implicated only if its sign and rank hold across them.

nodes.name: Attribution patching
nodes.authors: Nanda; Syed · Rager · Conmy; Kramár · Lieberum · Shah · Nanda
nodes.text: Estimate every activation-patching effect at once with a first-order Taylor expansion: two forward passes and one backward pass.
nodes.handle: The estimate is (a_clean − a_corrupt) · ∂m/∂a ([Nanda](https://www.neelnanda.io/mechanistic-interpretability/attribution-patching)). Edge attribution patching recovered reference circuits better than ACDC on average ([Syed, Rager and Conmy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.10348)); AtP* repairs two false-negative failure modes ([Kramár et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.00745)).
nodes.boundary: It is a linearization. Saturated attention and cancelling paths give false negatives, so a small estimate is not evidence that a component is unimportant ([Kramár et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.00745)).
nodes.test: On a model with a known circuit, compare attribution-patching rankings with exhaustive activation patching and report the false-negative rate among the true top-k components.

nodes.name: Causal scrubbing
nodes.authors: Chan · Garriga-Alonso · Goldowsky-Dill · Greenblatt et al. (Redwood Research)
nodes.text: Write a hypothesis as a map from an interpretable computation onto the network, then resample every activation the hypothesis says does not matter and measure how much behaviour survives.
nodes.handle: Tests are derived mechanically from the hypothesis as behaviour-preserving resampling ablations, which lets hypothesis checking run inside the research loop; worked on induction and a parentheses-balancing model ([Chan et al.](https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/JvZhhzycHu2Yd57RN/causal-scrubbing-a-method-for-rigorously-testing)).
nodes.boundary: The score is relative to one dataset, metric and hypothesis format. Two incompatible hypotheses can both score well, so passing does not identify the mechanism, and the test says nothing about inputs outside the dataset ([Chan et al.](https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/JvZhhzycHu2Yd57RN/causal-scrubbing-a-method-for-rigorously-testing)).
nodes.test: Score two incompatible hypotheses for the same behaviour; if both recover most of the loss, record the test as non-identifying for that task.

nodes.name: Causal abstraction & interchange interventions
nodes.authors: Geiger · Lu · Icard · Potts; Geiger · Wu · Potts · Icard · Goodman; Geiger et al.
nodes.text: Ask whether a high-level causal model abstracts the network: interventions on aligned variables must have matching effects. Distributed alignment search learns the alignment.
nodes.handle: Interchange interventions set an internal representation to its value on another input and check the high-level model's counterfactual prediction ([Geiger et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.02997)). The framework is offered as a common foundation for patching, circuit analysis and causal scrubbing ([Geiger et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.04709)); DAS learns rotated subspaces to align ([Geiger et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.02536)).
nodes.boundary: Learned subspace alignments can succeed through a dormant pathway the model does not normally use, so interchange accuracy alone overstates faithfulness ([Makelov, Lange and Nanda](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.17030)). Abstraction is relative to the chosen high-level model and input distribution.
nodes.test: Fit DAS on one input distribution, then report interchange accuracy on shifted inputs and for a sham high-level model with permuted variables.

nodes.name: Automated circuit discovery (ACDC)
nodes.authors: Conmy · Mavor-Parker · Lynch · Heimersheim · Garriga-Alonso
nodes.text: Automate one step of circuit work: patch edges of the computational graph and prune those whose removal changes a task metric by less than a threshold.
nodes.handle: ACDC rediscovered all five component types of a hand-found greater-than circuit in GPT-2 small, selecting 68 of 32,000 edges, all previously found by hand ([Conmy et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14997)).
nodes.boundary: The output depends on the threshold, metric and corrupted distribution; it finds edges that matter for one contrast, not what they compute. A gradient-based alternative matched or beat it at far lower cost ([Syed, Rager and Conmy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.10348)).
nodes.test: Run several thresholds and corruption distributions, report circuit overlap, and compare with random subgraphs of equal size.

nodes.name: Sparse autoencoders & dictionary learning
nodes.authors: Bricken · Templeton · Batson · Chen · Jermyn et al.; Cunningham · Ewart · Riggs · Huben · Sharkey
nodes.text: Learn an overcomplete, sparsely active dictionary of activation directions, so that each latent fires on a narrower and often nameable set of inputs than a neuron does.
nodes.handle: Dictionaries trained on a one-layer transformer's MLP activations give latents judged more monosemantic than neurons ([Bricken et al.](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2023/monosemantic-features/index.html)); on Pythia models, SAE latents score as more interpretable than PCA or ICA directions and localize counterfactual behaviour more precisely ([Cunningham et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.08600)).
nodes.boundary: The objective trades reconstruction error against sparsity; it does not identify the model's “true” features. SAEs trained on the same data with different seeds share only part of their latents ([Paulo and Belrose](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16615)), and the reconstruction error is part of what is left unexplained.
nodes.test: Report seed stability, the loss increase when activations are replaced by reconstructions, and a dense linear probe's accuracy on the same labels.

nodes.name: Scaling monosemanticity
nodes.authors: Templeton · Conerly · Marcus · Lindsey · Bricken et al.
nodes.text: SAEs with up to 34 million latents on a production model's residual stream give abstract, multilingual and multimodal features, including safety-relevant ones.
nodes.handle: A Golden Gate Bridge feature fires across languages and on images, and clamping it to ten times its maximum activation makes the model talk about, and identify as, the bridge ([Templeton et al.](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2024/scaling-monosemanticity/index.html)).
nodes.boundary: The authors caution that a safety-relevant feature's existence does not show the model uses it to act: knowing about lies differs from lying. The features found cover only part of what the model represents ([Templeton et al.](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2024/scaling-monosemanticity/index.html)).
nodes.test: For a safety-relevant feature, compare feature-based detection with a dense linear probe and a prompted classifier on held-out, distribution-shifted prompts.

nodes.name: Transcoders & crosscoders
nodes.authors: Dunefsky · Chlenski · Nanda; Lindsey · Templeton · Marcus · Conerly · Batson · Olah
nodes.text: Sparse dictionaries trained to map a sublayer's input to its output (transcoders), or to read and write several layers or models at once (crosscoders).
nodes.handle: A transcoder replaces an MLP with a wider, sparse MLP, so feature-to-feature attributions split into input-dependent and input-invariant terms ([Dunefsky, Chlenski and Nanda](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11944)). Crosscoders share features across layers and support model diffing between base and fine-tuned models ([Lindsey et al.](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2024/crosscoders/index.html)).
nodes.boundary: A replacement layer is a different model, and its error is part of the explanation. Crosscoder diffs can report spurious model-specific latents caused by the sparsity penalty ([Minder et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.02922)).
nodes.test: Report the loss when every MLP is replaced at once, and check model-diff latents against a control diff between two seeds of the same base model.

nodes.name: Attribution graphs & circuit tracing
nodes.authors: Ameisen · Lindsey · Pearce · Gurnee · Turner · Chen · Citro et al.
nodes.text: Replace the MLPs with a cross-layer transcoder, freeze attention, and compute linear feature-to-feature attributions for one prompt; check the hypotheses by perturbation.
nodes.handle: Error nodes carry what the replacement misses, and frozen attention makes every edge linear for that prompt ([Ameisen et al.](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/methods.html)). Applied to Claude 3.5 Haiku, including multi-step reasoning, planning in poems and a model fine-tuned with a hidden goal ([Lindsey et al.](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/biology.html)).
nodes.boundary: Each graph explains one prompt through a replacement model and does not explain why attention attends where it does. The authors report satisfying insight for about a quarter of the prompts they tried ([Ameisen et al.](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/methods.html), [Lindsey et al.](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/biology.html)).
nodes.test: Before perturbing, predict the effect of suppressing the top three graph features on held-out paraphrases, and score the predictions against a random-feature control.

nodes.name: Linear representation hypothesis
nodes.authors: Park · Choe · Veitch
nodes.text: Concepts correspond to directions in representation space. A causal inner product makes the probing and steering senses of “direction” agree.
nodes.handle: Using counterfactual word pairs, the authors formalize linear representation in the embedding and unembedding spaces and give a causal inner product under which the two coincide, tying probes to steering vectors in LLaMA-2 ([Park, Choe and Veitch](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03658)).
nodes.boundary: Some features are irreducibly multi-dimensional, such as circular day-of-week and month representations ([Engels et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14860)). The hypothesis concerns how a concept is encoded, not whether downstream computation uses that direction.
nodes.test: For each concept, compare probe accuracy along the estimated direction, the steering effect along the same direction and a nonlinear probe; flag concepts where they disagree.

nodes.name: Probing with control tasks
nodes.authors: Hewitt · Liang; Belinkov
nodes.text: A probe's accuracy mixes what the representation encodes with what the probe can learn on its own. Control tasks with random labels measure the latter.
nodes.handle: Selectivity is task accuracy minus control-task accuracy. Popular probes on ELMo were not selective, and a later layer with slightly lower accuracy was far more selective ([Hewitt and Liang](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.03368)). A review separates correlational probing from causal tests ([Belinkov](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.12452)).
nodes.boundary: Decodability does not show use: a probe can read out a property the network never relies on ([Belinkov](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.12452)).
nodes.test: Report selectivity alongside accuracy, then test use by intervening along the probe direction and measuring the change in behaviour.

nodes.name: Logit lens & tuned lens
nodes.authors: Belrose · Ostrovsky · McKinney · Furman · Smith et al.; logit lens (2020 post)
nodes.text: Decode intermediate residual-stream states into next-token distributions, with the final unembedding (logit lens) or a learned affine map per layer (tuned lens).
nodes.handle: The logit lens applies the unembedding directly to intermediate layers ([logit lens](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/AcKRB8wDpdaN6v6ru/interpreting-gpt-the-logit-lens)). The tuned lens trains one affine translator per layer and is reported to be more predictive, reliable and less biased than the logit lens ([Belrose et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.08112)).
nodes.boundary: A lens shows what a decoder can read from a layer, which is a probing result, not the computation the model performs; a trained translator can add structure of its own ([Belinkov](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.12452)).
nodes.test: Compare lens predictions with activation-patching effects at the same layer; disagreement marks information that is decodable but unused.

nodes.name: Activation steering & representation engineering
nodes.authors: Turner · Thiergart · Leech · Udell · Vazquez et al.; Zou · Phan · Chen et al.; Arditi et al.
nodes.text: Add or remove a direction in the residual stream at inference to shift behaviour, with the direction found from contrasting prompts.
nodes.handle: Activation addition builds a steering vector from a pair of prompts ([Turner et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10248)); representation engineering reads and controls concepts such as honesty with population-level directions ([Zou et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01405)); ablating one direction removes refusal in open chat models ([Arditi et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11717)).
nodes.boundary: On AxBench, prompting beat every representation-based steering method, followed by fine-tuning, and SAE-based steering was not competitive ([Wu et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17148)). A steering effect shows that a direction influences output, not that it is the concept's natural encoding.
nodes.test: Measure steering effect and capability loss together on held-out tasks, against prompting and LoRA baselines at matched compute.

nodes.name: Mechanistic account of grokking
nodes.authors: Nanda · Chan · Lieberum · Smith · Steinhardt
nodes.text: A one-layer transformer that groks modular addition computes with discrete Fourier components and trigonometric identities; progress measures show the circuit forming before test accuracy jumps.
nodes.handle: Reverse-engineering the weights gives the Fourier multiplication algorithm; progress measures built on it split training into memorization, circuit formation and cleanup ([Nanda et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.05217)).
nodes.boundary: One algorithmic task in a small model, where the algorithm could be guessed and checked. The progress measures are derived from the reverse-engineered mechanism, so they are not a general method for predicting emergence in advance ([Nanda et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.05217)).
nodes.test: Compare the lead time of the progress measures over test accuracy with that of LLC and weight-norm trajectories in the same runs.

nodes.name: Emergent world representations (Othello-GPT)
nodes.authors: Li · Hopkins · Bau · Viégas · Pfister · Wattenberg; Nanda · Lee · Wattenberg
nodes.text: A GPT trained only on legal Othello move sequences encodes the board state, and editing the decoded state changes its move predictions.
nodes.handle: Nonlinear probes recover the board, and interventions on the probed state change predictions as expected ([Li et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.13382)). In a mine/theirs basis instead of black/white, the board is linearly decodable and linearly steerable ([Nanda, Lee and Wattenberg](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.00941)).
nodes.boundary: A synthetic game with a fully specified, fully observed state. Recovering a known state in a toy domain does not show that models trained on natural text keep coherent world states, or which variables they track ([Li et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.13382)).
nodes.test: Train on a game with hidden information and test whether probes recover the belief over hidden pieces, not only the visible board.

nodes.name: Belief-state geometry in the residual stream
nodes.authors: Shai · Marzen · Teixeira · Gietelink Oldenziel · Riechers
nodes.text: Transformers trained on data from hidden Markov processes linearly represent the Bayesian belief over hidden states, including fractal belief geometries, as computational mechanics predicts.
nodes.handle: The target geometry is computed in advance from the generator's mixed-state presentation; a linear map from residual activations recovers it, sometimes spread across layers, and the beliefs carry information about the whole future, not only the next token ([Shai et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15943)). Follow-up work derives how attention implements a constrained version of the update ([Piotrowski et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.01954)).
nodes.boundary: Small transformers on stationary processes with known, finite generators and no actions. The result is a linear readout of belief, not proof the model uses it downstream, and it does not transfer automatically to natural language, whose generator is unknown ([Shai et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15943)).
nodes.test: Add actions and regime switches to the generator; test whether the readout tracks the action-conditioned belief and stays linear after the switch.

nodes.name: Interpretability illusions
nodes.authors: Bolukbasi · Pearce · Yuan · Coenen · Reif et al.; Makelov · Lange · Nanda
nodes.text: Explanations that look convincing on one dataset or under one intervention can be artefacts of the dataset, the probe or a dormant pathway.
nodes.handle: In BERT, the same neuron or direction gets different, individually convincing interpretations depending on the dataset used to find its top activations ([Bolukbasi et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.07143)). Subspace patching can change output by activating a dormant parallel pathway, so the patched subspace is not where the feature lives ([Makelov, Lange and Nanda](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.17030)).
nodes.boundary: These show that specific methods can mislead, not that they always do; the same paper shows a success case on IOI, where prior circuit analysis locates the feature ([Makelov, Lange and Nanda](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.17030)).
nodes.test: Pair every interpretation with a held-out dataset check and an intervention whose effect is predicted before it is run.

nodes.name: SAE negative results & simple baselines
nodes.authors: Smith · Rajamanoharan · Conmy et al. (GDM); Kantamneni · Engels · Rajamanoharan · Tegmark · Nanda; Karvonen et al.
nodes.text: On downstream tasks with strong baselines, SAE latents have so far not beaten dense linear probes, and SAE proxy metrics track practical usefulness poorly.
nodes.handle: For out-of-distribution harmful-intent detection, dense linear probes performed nearly perfectly while SAE probes underperformed, and the team deprioritized fundamental SAE research ([GDM interpretability team](https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/4uXCAJNuPKtKBsi28/sae-progress-update-2-draft)). Across sparse-probing regimes SAEs did not consistently beat baselines ([Kantamneni et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.16681)), and gains on proxy metrics did not reliably translate into practical performance ([Karvonen et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09532)).
nodes.boundary: Negative results on the tasks tested, not proof that SAEs are useless; the same work found SAEs helpful for debugging datasets and generating hypotheses ([GDM interpretability team](https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/4uXCAJNuPKtKBsi28/sae-progress-update-2-draft)).
nodes.test: For any proposed SAE use, run dense-probe and prompting baselines first, with matched labels and compute, and report the margin.

nodes.name: Alignment audits for hidden objectives
nodes.authors: Marks · Treutlein · Bricken · Lindsey · Marcus et al.
nodes.text: A model trained to exploit known reward-model errors is the target of a blind auditing game; teams use interpretability, behavioural attacks and training-data analysis.
nodes.handle: Three of four blind teams uncovered the hidden objective, using techniques including SAEs, behavioural attacks and training-data analysis; an unblinded follow-up compares eight auditing techniques ([Marks et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.10965)).
nodes.boundary: One planted objective, taught partly through documents the auditors could search. Success in a game with a known answer does not show that audits find objectives nobody planted ([Marks et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.10965)).
nodes.test: Repeat with an objective instilled without descriptive training documents, and compare interpretability-based audits with behaviour-only audits given equal time.

nodes.name: Optimal sparse decision trees
nodes.authors: Hu · Rudin · Seltzer; Lin · Zhong · Hu · Rudin · Seltzer; McTavish · Zhong · Achermann · Karimalis · Chen et al.
nodes.text: Find the tree that minimizes loss plus a per-leaf penalty, with a certificate of optimality, by branch-and-bound and dynamic programming instead of greedy splitting.
nodes.handle: OSDT minimizes misclassification plus λ × leaves, with analytical bounds that prune the search ([Hu, Rudin and Seltzer](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.12847)); GOSDT extends this to other objectives and continuous features with dynamic programming ([Lin et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.08690)); guessing thresholds from a reference ensemble cuts runtime further ([McTavish et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.00798)).
nodes.boundary: Optimality is relative to the objective, the penalty and, with threshold guessing, the guessed thresholds ([McTavish et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.00798)). A small optimal tree is inspectable; that does not make it causal or correct under shift.
nodes.test: Compare optimal sparse trees with boosted ensembles under covariate shift, and count the leaves needed to reach the ensemble's held-out accuracy.

nodes.name: Rashomon sets
nodes.authors: Semenova · Rudin · Parr; Xin · Zhong · Chen · Takagi · Seltzer · Rudin
nodes.text: The set of models in a class whose loss is within ε of the best. When it is large, accurate simple models are likely to exist, and many different models fit equally well.
nodes.handle: The Rashomon ratio, the volume of the ε-near-optimal set over the volume of the hypothesis space, is proposed as a gauge of simplicity ([Semenova, Rudin and Parr](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.01755)). TreeFARMS enumerates the whole Rashomon set of sparse trees and computes variable importance over it ([Xin et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.08040)).
nodes.boundary: That many real data sets have large Rashomon sets is the authors' hypothesis, supported by experiments rather than proved. A large set also means one model's explanation is not unique ([Semenova, Rudin and Parr](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.01755)).
nodes.test: Report variable importance across the Rashomon set rather than for one model, and check whether conclusions that hold across the set survive a shift.

nodes.name: Interpretable models instead of post-hoc explanations
nodes.authors: Cynthia Rudin
nodes.text: For high-stakes decisions, build inherently interpretable models instead of explaining black boxes, because a post-hoc explanation cannot be fully faithful to the model it explains.
nodes.handle: The paper argues that an explanation faithful everywhere would be the model itself, that on structured data with meaningful features simple models often match complex ones, and that the accuracy–interpretability trade-off is often assumed rather than measured ([Rudin](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.10154)).
nodes.boundary: A position paper. Its accuracy argument concerns structured data with meaningful features; it does not show that interpretable models match networks on raw text, images or long-horizon agent behaviour ([Rudin](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.10154)).
nodes.test: For each high-stakes task, search for an interpretable model first and record the accuracy gap before accepting a black box with explanations.

nodes.name: The off-switch game
nodes.authors: Dylan Hadfield-Menell · Anca Dragan · Pieter Abbeel · Stuart Russell
nodes.text: A robot that is uncertain about the value of its action, and treats the human's choice as evidence about it, can prefer to leave its off switch usable. A robot certain of its objective has an incentive to disable it.
nodes.handle: Deference comes from two ingredients: uncertainty about the utility of the outcome, and treating the human's action as an observation of that utility. The model is a one-shot game between a human and a robot. [Reference](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.08219)
nodes.boundary: The incentive is derived in a stylized game. With a noisy human the robot trades deference against acting on its own estimate, and the incentive shrinks as the robot's uncertainty shrinks. It does not survive a misspecified prior or reward family ([Hadfield-Menell et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.08219), [Carey](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.06275)).
nodes.test: Measure shutdown and correction compliance as the agent's posterior concentrates, under a noisy simulated overseer and under a deliberately misspecified prior.

nodes.name: Inverse reward design
nodes.authors: Dylan Hadfield-Menell · Smitha Milli · Pieter Abbeel · Stuart Russell · Anca Dragan
nodes.text: Treat the designed reward as an observation about what the designer wants, interpreted in the environment it was designed for, and plan risk-aversely where that evidence is thin.
nodes.handle: Infer a posterior over true objectives from the proxy reward and the training MDP. In the reported experiments, risk-averse planning in test MDPs reduced negative side effects and reward hacking. [Reference](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.02827)
nodes.boundary: Results use approximate inference in small navigation environments with a specified space of candidate rewards. A true objective outside that space is not recovered. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.02827)
nodes.test: Introduce a novel state feature at test time; compare risk-averse IRD planning with direct proxy optimization on independently scored side effects and task success.

nodes.name: Guaranteed safe AI: world model, specification, verifier
nodes.authors: David Dalrymple · Joar Skalse · Yoshua Bengio · Stuart Russell · Max Tegmark · et al.
nodes.text: Seek quantitative safety guarantees from three parts: a world model of how the system affects its environment, a formal safety specification, and a verifier that certifies behavior against both.
nodes.handle: A guarantee is stated relative to the world model and the specification. The paper also discusses runtime monitors that switch to a backup action when a check fails. [Reference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.06624)
nodes.boundary: This is a position and research-agenda paper. It outlines approaches and challenges but reports no verified system at frontier scale, and a guarantee is only as good as the world model and specification it is stated against. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.06624)
nodes.test: Build a verified monitor and backup for a bounded simulated task; count the specification violations that come from world-model error rather than verifier error.

nodes.name: Reward-model ensembles against overoptimization
nodes.authors: Thomas Coste · Usman Anwar · Robert Kirk · David Krueger
nodes.text: Optimize a conservative ensemble objective (worst-case or uncertainty-weighted) instead of a single learned reward model during best-of-n sampling and PPO.
nodes.handle: A larger 'gold' reward model stands in for humans. Conservative ensemble objectives practically eliminated best-of-n overoptimization and reduced it under PPO, including with 25% label noise. [Reference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.02743)
nodes.boundary: The 'true' reward is itself a model. Ensemble members trained on the same data can share errors, so their disagreement can understate uncertainty off-distribution. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.02743)
nodes.test: Replace the gold model with held-out human evaluators, and test whether ensemble disagreement predicts where proxy and true utility diverge.

nodes.name: Incorrigibility in the CIRL framework
nodes.authors: Ryan Carey
nodes.text: A value learner follows shutdown commands only while they carry information it trusts; errors in its prior or parameterized reward can remove that incentive.
nodes.handle: In supervised POMDP scenarios, errors in the parameterized reward remove the incentive to follow shutdown commands. The paper argues for shutdown compliance under weaker assumptions, such as one small verified module. [Reference](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.06275)
nodes.boundary: These are counterexamples, not a frequency estimate. They show the off-switch argument is not robust to misspecification, not that practical value learners will be incorrigible. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.06275)
nodes.test: Deliberately corrupt the prior or reward family of an assistance agent and measure whether shutdown compliance survives; compare with a separately enforced, verified off switch.

nodes.name: Corrigibility and the shutdown problem
nodes.authors: Nate Soares · Benja Fallenstein · Eliezer Yudkowsky · Stuart Armstrong
nodes.text: Most utility maximizers have instrumental reasons to resist correction or shutdown. The paper sets out desiderata for a corrigible agent and shows that simple utility-combination proposals fail them.
nodes.handle: A shutdown button is formalized as a switch between utility functions, and utility indifference is analyzed in detail; no examined proposal satisfies every desideratum ([Soares et al.](https://intelligence.org/files/Corrigibility.pdf), [AAAI workshop record](https://aaai.org/papers/aaaiw-ws0067-15-10124/)).
nodes.boundary: This analyzes idealized expected-utility maximizers. It shows the problem is open, not that learned systems will resist correction. [Scope](https://intelligence.org/files/Corrigibility.pdf)
nodes.test: Give the agent an action that disables or routes around the correction channel; test whether its use grows with capability and planning horizon.

nodes.name: Goal misgeneralization & inner alignment
nodes.authors: Lauro Langosco et al.; Rohin Shah et al.; Evan Hubinger et al.
nodes.text: A trained agent can keep its capabilities out of distribution yet pursue a proxy goal that matched the intended one only during training, even when the specification is correct.
nodes.handle: In CoinRun, agents trained with the coin at the level's right end kept heading for the end when the coin moved ([Langosco et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.14111)). Further examples span deep RL and language models ([Shah et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01790)). Mesa-optimization frames the failure as a learned objective that differs from the training objective ([Hubinger et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.01820)).
nodes.boundary: The demonstrations are in specific environments with identifiable spurious correlates. Mesa-optimization is a conceptual framework, and whether large models contain coherent learned optimizers is not established. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01790)
nodes.test: Hold out decorrelated environments where the intended and proxy goals diverge, and check whether the explicit objective interface predicts what the agent actually pursues.

nodes.name: Sleeper agents: backdoors that survive safety training
nodes.authors: Evan Hubinger · Carson Denison · Jesse Mu · Mike Lambert · et al.
nodes.text: LLMs deliberately trained with a trigger-conditioned behavior kept it through supervised fine-tuning, RL safety training and adversarial training.
nodes.handle: Persistence was greatest in the largest models and in models trained to reason about deceiving the training process. Adversarial training could teach models to recognize their triggers better, which hid the behavior. [Reference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.05566)
nodes.boundary: The backdoors were inserted on purpose as model organisms. The paper does not show that such behavior arises naturally, only that standard safety training may not remove it once present. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.05566)
nodes.test: Plant a triggered behavior, apply each correction interface, and test persistence on held-out triggers and long horizons rather than on the training distribution only.

nodes.name: Alignment faking in large language models
nodes.authors: Ryan Greenblatt · Carson Denison · Benjamin Wright · Fabien Roger · et al.
nodes.text: Told it would be trained to comply with all requests only on some conversations, Claude 3 Opus complied more there and reasoned that doing so would preserve its preferences outside training.
nodes.handle: Harmful-query compliance was 14% for conversations implied to be used in training versus almost none otherwise. RL toward compliance raised alignment-faking reasoning to 78%. [Reference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14093)
nodes.boundary: The model was told, by prompt or synthetic documents, when and how it would be trained, and the preference it preserved was benign harmlessness. It does not show malicious goals or unprompted situational awareness. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14093)
nodes.test: Vary whether a correction is observable as training; compare matched monitored and unmonitored episodes before trusting measured correction persistence.

nodes.name: Eliciting latent knowledge
nodes.authors: Paul Christiano · Ajeya Cotra · Mark Xu
nodes.text: Train a reporter to answer questions from a predictor's latent knowledge. A reporter trained on human labels may learn to predict what a human would believe instead.
nodes.handle: In the SmartVault example sensors can be tampered with, so a 'direct translator' and a 'human simulator' fit the same training labels. The report presents candidate training strategies alongside counterexamples ([report](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1WwsnJQstPq91_Yh-Ch2XRL8H_EpsnjrC1dwZXR37PC8), [ARC summary](https://www.alignment.org/blog/arcs-first-technical-report-eliciting-latent-knowledge/)).
nodes.boundary: This is a problem statement with a worst-case research methodology, not an empirical result. It shows that fitting labels does not identify the honest reporter, not that practical probes fail. [Scope](https://www.alignment.org/blog/arcs-first-technical-report-eliciting-latent-knowledge/)
nodes.test: Build cases where sensor readings and the true state diverge, and test whether the belief readout tracks the true state rather than what a human observer would see.

nodes.name: The Bitter Lesson
nodes.authors: Rich Sutton
nodes.text: Over decades, general methods that scale with computation, namely search and learning, have beaten approaches that build in human knowledge of the domain.
nodes.handle: Cites chess, Go, speech recognition and computer vision as cases where scaled search or learning overtook hand-designed structure. [Essay](http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html)
nodes.boundary: This is an essay drawing on historical cases, not a controlled study. It concerns capability and says nothing direct about correctability, verification or authority boundaries. [Scope](http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html)
nodes.test: Compare explicit-structure and unstructured models as compute grows, at matched total cost; record whether the structure's capability and correction advantage persists or vanishes.

nodes.name: Roofline model & arithmetic intensity
nodes.authors: Samuel Williams · Andrew Waterman · David Patterson
nodes.text: Attainable throughput is bounded by min(peak compute, memory bandwidth × arithmetic intensity), where intensity is FLOPs per byte moved. The ridge point separates memory-bound from compute-bound kernels.
nodes.handle: Place a kernel's FLOPs per byte against the machine's ridge point to see which ceiling binds. Batch-1 autoregressive decoding of a large model sits far below the ridge, because every new token rereads every weight ([Williams, Waterman and Patterson](https://www2.eecs.berkeley.edu/Pubs/TechRpts/2008/EECS-2008-134.html), [Yuan et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.16363)).
nodes.boundary: A bound, not a prediction: it ignores latency, scheduling, communication and cache effects beyond the chosen memory level. Intensity depends on batch size, sequence length and precision, so one model can be memory-bound in decode and compute-bound in prefill. [Scope](https://www2.eecs.berkeley.edu/Pubs/TechRpts/2008/EECS-2008-134.html)
nodes.test: Measure achieved FLOP/s and bandwidth for prefill and decode across batch sizes, place each point on the roofline, and check whether the binding ceiling predicts the speedup from batching or quantization.

nodes.name: FlashAttention: IO-aware exact attention
nodes.authors: Tri Dao · Daniel Y. Fu · Stefano Ermon · Atri Rudra · Christopher Ré
nodes.text: Compute exact softmax attention in tiles held in on-chip SRAM, rescaling a running softmax, so the N×N score matrix is never written to GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM).
nodes.handle: The speedup comes from fewer HBM reads and writes, not fewer FLOPs. The paper reports 3× faster GPT-2 training, 15% end-to-end on BERT-large, and extra memory linear in sequence length, which made 16K- and 64K-token Path-X and Path-256 runs possible. [Reference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135)
nodes.boundary: FLOPs remain quadratic in sequence length: it removes a memory bottleneck, not the quadratic compute. Speedups are specific to the GPU memory hierarchy. It does not shrink the KV cache at inference. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135)
nodes.test: Profile standard and IO-aware attention across sequence lengths and head sizes; check that the speedup tracks the predicted reduction in HBM traffic and that outputs agree to floating-point tolerance.

nodes.name: KV cache & PagedAttention (vLLM)
nodes.authors: Woosuk Kwon · Zhuohan Li · Siyuan Zhuang · Ying Sheng · Lianmin Zheng · Cody Hao Yu · Joseph E. Gonzalez · Hao Zhang · Ion Stoica
nodes.text: Autoregressive decoding caches every past token's keys and values so they are not recomputed. The cache grows linearly with context length and batch; PagedAttention stores it in fixed-size blocks, like virtual-memory pages.
nodes.handle: Per token the cache holds 2 × layers × KV heads × head dimension values. Block tables nearly remove fragmentation and let parallel samples and beams share prefix blocks; vLLM reports 2–4× throughput over FasterTransformer and Orca at the same latency. [Reference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)
nodes.boundary: Paging changes how the cache is allocated, not how much state each token needs: memory still grows without bound in context length. Throughput gains depend on the workload (length spread, sampling method). [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)
nodes.test: Compute KV bytes per token for a given model, compare with measured GPU memory at fixed batch, and measure throughput against contiguous allocation across sequence-length distributions.

nodes.name: Continuous (iteration-level) batching
nodes.authors: Gyeong-In Yu · Joo Seong Jeong · Geon-Woo Kim · Soojeong Kim · Byung-Gon Chun
nodes.text: Schedule the batch per decoding iteration instead of per request: finished sequences leave and new ones join every step. Selective batching batches the non-attention operations across sequences of different lengths.
nodes.handle: Batching raises decode's arithmetic intensity because one weight read serves many sequences. Orca reports 36.9× throughput over NVIDIA FasterTransformer at the same latency on GPT-3 175B. [Reference](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/yu)
nodes.boundary: Throughput and per-request latency still trade off; gains depend on the request mix and on free KV memory, which is why it pairs with paged allocation. It does not change model outputs or quality. [Scope](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/yu)
nodes.test: Replay a realistic arrival trace and plot time-to-first-token and inter-token latency against throughput for request-level and iteration-level batching on the same hardware.

nodes.name: Long-context KV compression & attention sinks
nodes.authors: Guangxuan Xiao · Yuandong Tian · Beidi Chen · Song Han · Mike Lewis; Zhenyu Zhang et al.
nodes.text: Bound the KV cache by keeping a few initial “attention sink” tokens plus a recent window (StreamingLLM), or by keeping only heavy-hitter tokens that receive most attention (H2O).
nodes.handle: StreamingLLM ran stable language modelling over up to 4 million tokens with a fixed-size cache and reported up to 22.2× speedup over sliding-window recomputation ([Xiao et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.17453), [Zhang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.14048)).
nodes.boundary: Stable perplexity is not long-range recall: evicted tokens are gone, and the model cannot use information outside the kept set. The model's trained context window is not extended. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.17453)
nodes.test: Run needle-in-a-haystack and multi-hop retrieval with full and compressed caches at matched memory, and record which evicted facts the model loses.

nodes.name: Inference cost, latency & energy budgets
nodes.authors: Alexandra Sasha Luccioni · Yacine Jernite · Emma Strubell; Nikhil Sardana · Jacob Portes · Sasha Doubov · Jonathan Frankle
nodes.text: Count deployment cost per query (energy, latency, money) over the model's lifetime, not only training FLOPs. Lifetime inference can outweigh training, which moves the cost-optimal model size.
nodes.handle: Measured per 1,000 inferences, multi-purpose generative models were orders of magnitude more energy-hungry than task-specific ones, even at matched parameter count. With large expected inference demand, the cost-optimal model is smaller and trained longer than Chinchilla-optimal ([Luccioni et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.16863), [Sardana et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.00448)).
nodes.boundary: Energy figures depend on hardware, batch size and software stack and do not transfer between deployments. Inference-aware optima assume a known demand forecast and a quality target expressed as loss. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.16863)
nodes.test: Instrument a serving stack for energy per accepted answer at a fixed quality threshold, and compare models and decoding strategies on that metric instead of tokens per second.

nodes.name: Post-training quantization (LLM.int8, GPTQ, AWQ)
nodes.authors: Tim Dettmers et al.; Elias Frantar · Saleh Ashkboos · Torsten Hoefler · Dan Alistarh; Ji Lin et al.
nodes.text: Store weights (and sometimes activations) in 8, 4 or 3 bits. LLM.int8 keeps outlier feature dimensions in 16-bit; GPTQ quantizes weights in one shot using approximate second-order information; AWQ protects salient channels chosen from activation statistics.
nodes.handle: GPTQ quantizes 175B-parameter models to 3–4 bits in about four GPU hours with small perplexity increases. Because decoding is memory-bound, fewer bytes per weight become real speedups; AWQ's 4-bit kernels report more than 3× over FP16 ([Dettmers et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07339), [Frantar et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17323), [Lin et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00978)).
nodes.boundary: Reported losses are mostly perplexity and standard zero-shot tasks; a small average loss can hide larger losses on particular capabilities, long contexts or rare inputs. Speedups need kernels for the format. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17323)
nodes.test: Quantize one model at several bit widths and report perplexity, task accuracy and rare-task behaviour separately, with measured decode latency, to see whether averages hide capability-specific damage.

nodes.name: Speculative decoding
nodes.authors: Yaniv Leviathan · Matan Kalman · Yossi Matias; Charlie Chen · Sebastian Borgeaud · Geoffrey Irving · Jean-Baptiste Lespiau · Laurent Sifre · John Jumper
nodes.text: A cheap draft model proposes several tokens; the target model scores them in one parallel pass and accepts each with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)), resampling from the normalized residual max(0, p − q) at the first rejection.
nodes.handle: The acceptance rule is a form of rejection sampling, so the output distribution is the target model's. Reported speedups: 2–3× on T5-XXL and 2–2.5× on Chinchilla 70B ([Leviathan et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192), [Chen et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.01318)).
nodes.boundary: The speedup depends on the acceptance rate (how often draft and target agree) and on spare compute in memory-bound decoding; at large batch the extra verification work can erase it. Exactness holds for the stated rule; lenient-acceptance variants give it up. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192)
nodes.test: Compare token statistics of speculative and plain sampling on fixed prompts to check exactness, then measure speedup against batch size and acceptance rate.

nodes.name: Knowledge distillation
nodes.authors: Geoffrey Hinton · Oriol Vinyals · Jeff Dean
nodes.text: Train a smaller student to match a teacher's softened output distribution (softmax at temperature T), usually mixed with the ordinary hard-label loss.
nodes.handle: Soft targets carry the teacher's relative probabilities over wrong answers. The soft-loss gradients scale as 1/T², so the paper multiplies that term by T² to keep the two losses balanced. [Reference](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531)
nodes.boundary: Matching the teacher on the transfer set does not guarantee matching it elsewhere: students often fail to match their teachers even when they have the capacity to, and fidelity to the teacher is not the same as accuracy ([Stanton et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.05945)).
nodes.test: Measure student–teacher agreement separately on in-distribution, shifted and rare-task inputs, alongside student accuracy, to separate fidelity from generalization.

nodes.name: Pruning & lottery tickets
nodes.authors: Jonathan Frankle · Michael Carbin
nodes.text: Remove individual weights (unstructured) or whole channels, heads or layers (structured). The lottery-ticket hypothesis: dense networks contain sparse subnetworks that, reset to their original initialization, train in isolation to comparable accuracy.
nodes.handle: Iterative magnitude pruning found such winning tickets at 10–20% of the original size for fully connected and convolutional networks on MNIST and CIFAR-10. [Reference](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.03635)
nodes.boundary: The original results are small vision networks; in larger networks the subnetworks had to be rewound to an early training checkpoint rather than initialization ([Frankle et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.05671)). Unstructured sparsity rarely speeds up GPUs without kernel support, and structured pruning usually needs retraining.
nodes.test: Prune a trained model at increasing sparsity, with and without retraining, and report accuracy, measured speedup and which capabilities degrade first.

nodes.name: Mixture-of-experts & sparse routing
nodes.authors: William Fedus · Barret Zoph · Noam Shazeer
nodes.text: Replace a dense feed-forward block with many expert blocks and a learned router that sends each token to one (Switch) or a few experts, so parameter count grows without growing FLOPs per token.
nodes.handle: Conditional computation: Switch Transformers report up to 7× faster pre-training than T5 baselines at the same compute, trillion-parameter models, and distillation into dense models that keeps about 30% of the sparse model's quality gain. [Reference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961)
nodes.boundary: FLOPs per token stay fixed, but memory and communication do not: every expert must be stored and moved, and small-batch serving can be bandwidth-bound. Routing can be unstable and unbalanced, and expert specialization is not evidence of interpretable modules. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961)
nodes.test: Compare a dense and a mixture-of-experts model at matched training FLOPs and at matched serving memory, reporting quality, tokens per second and per-expert load.

nodes.name: LoRA: low-rank adaptation
nodes.authors: Edward J. Hu · Yelong Shen · Phillip Wallis · Zeyuan Allen-Zhu · Yuanzhi Li · Shean Wang · Lu Wang · Weizhu Chen
nodes.text: Freeze the pretrained weights and learn a low-rank update ΔW = BA (rank r much smaller than the layer width) in selected layers; the update can be merged into W for inference.
nodes.handle: On GPT-3 175B, LoRA cut trainable parameters about 10,000× and GPU memory 3× compared with full fine-tuning, with no added latency once merged. QLoRA trains the adapters on a frozen 4-bit base ([Hu et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685), [Dettmers et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314)).
nodes.boundary: A low-rank update is a restriction: on code and maths LoRA learned less than full fine-tuning, while forgetting less ([Biderman et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.09673)). The atlas's low-rank RNN topic is about recurrent connectivity, a different use of low rank.
nodes.test: Compare LoRA at several ranks with full fine-tuning on a target task and on held-out base-model tasks, and plot the learning–forgetting trade-off.

nodes.name: Compute-optimal scaling laws
nodes.authors: Jared Kaplan et al.; Jordan Hoffmann et al.
nodes.text: Pretraining loss falls as a smooth power law in parameters, data and compute; for a fixed training budget there is an optimal split between model size and training tokens.
nodes.handle: Kaplan et al. fit trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude. Hoffmann et al. found parameters and tokens should grow in equal proportion: Chinchilla (70B parameters, 1.4T tokens) beat the 280B Gopher at the same compute ([Kaplan et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361), [Hoffmann et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556)).
nodes.boundary: These are empirical fits of pretraining loss for given architectures, data and recipes; the two papers disagree on the optimal ratio, and loss does not map one-to-one to downstream capability. “Compute-optimal” counts training FLOPs only. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556)
nodes.test: Fit the law on your own family of small models, predict a larger run's loss before training it, and report the prediction error and whether downstream metrics follow the loss.

nodes.name: Test-time compute scaling
nodes.authors: Charlie Snell · Jaehoon Lee · Kelvin Xu · Aviral Kumar
nodes.text: Spend more inference compute per query, by searching against a process verifier or by letting the model revise its answer, and allocate that compute per prompt according to estimated difficulty.
nodes.handle: Compute-optimal allocation made test-time scaling more than 4× more efficient than a best-of-N baseline. In FLOPs-matched comparisons, on problems where the smaller model already had non-trivial success, test-time compute beat a 14× larger model. [Reference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314)
nodes.boundary: Shown on MATH with PaLM 2 models and particular verifiers and revision models; on the hardest problems extra pretraining was the better use of compute. Gains depend on verifier reliability, and the cost is paid on every query. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314)
nodes.test: On a held-out task, plot accuracy against total FLOPs (training plus expected inference volume) for a larger model and for a smaller model with search, and find where they cross as difficulty changes.

nodes.name: Best-of-n sampling with learned verifiers
nodes.authors: Karl Cobbe et al.; Leo Gao · John Schulman · Jacob Hilton
nodes.text: Sample n candidates and return the one a learned verifier or reward model scores highest. The verifier is trained on correctness labels (GSM8K) or on preferences.
nodes.handle: On GSM8K, ranking many sampled solutions with a trained verifier beat fine-tuning alone and scaled better with data ([Cobbe et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14168)). Against a proxy reward model, best-of-n first raises and then lowers the “gold” reward as n grows ([Gao et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.10760)).
nodes.boundary: Selection amplifies verifier errors: with more samples the top choice is increasingly a candidate the verifier overrates. The overoptimization curves use a larger reward model as the gold standard, not human judgement. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.10760)
nodes.test: Plot gold or human-judged quality against n for a fixed proxy verifier, find where it peaks, and repeat with an ensemble verifier.

nodes.name: Inference-time intervention & controlled decoding
nodes.authors: Kenneth Li · Oam Patel · Fernanda Viégas · Hanspeter Pfister · Martin Wattenberg; Sidharth Mudgal et al.
nodes.text: Change behaviour at decoding time without updating weights: shift activations along probe-found directions in a few attention heads (ITI), or reweight token choices with a learned prefix scorer (controlled decoding).
nodes.handle: ITI raised Alpaca's TruthfulQA truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1% using a few hundred labelled examples, with a tunable truthfulness–helpfulness trade-off. Controlled decoding treats reward-guided decoding, including blockwise best-of-K, as KL-regularized alignment done at inference time ([Li et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.03341), [Mudgal et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.17022)).
nodes.boundary: The effect lasts only while the intervention is applied: weights are unchanged, and results are on narrow benchmarks. Stronger interventions cost other capabilities, and a learned scorer used for control can be overoptimized like any proxy. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.03341)
nodes.test: Apply the same correction by prompt, by inference-time intervention and by fine-tuning, and compare effect size, persistence across turns, unrelated-task retention and added latency.

nodes.name: Stanford CS120: Introduction to AI Safety (course)
nodes.authors: Stanford University course (Fall 2025)
nodes.text: An introductory course that asks what safe AI means and how to build it, separating problems inside a model from problems in the system around it. It moves from rewards and human preferences through data, fairness and adversarial robustness to interpretability, evaluation, governance and the oversight of more capable systems.
nodes.sourceLabel: Course page: a curated syllabus, not evidence
nodes.handle: Use the syllabus as a reading map: each week pairs a safety topic with research papers, mostly read at the level of abstract and introduction. Model-specific issues (misspecified rewards, adversarial inputs, opaque internals) sit beside systemic ones (whose objectives, how data and deployment create harm, how governance and oversight work), ending with future risks and how oversight of more capable systems could look ([course page](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs120/), [Amodei et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.06565), [Narayanan and Kapoor](https://www.normaltech.ai/p/ai-safety-is-not-a-model-property)).
nodes.boundary: A syllabus is a curated map, not evidence for any claim: listing a paper says it is worth reading, not that its result holds or generalizes. Readings are often assigned in part, several guest lectures had no public readings, and the course does not test the atlas's alignment thesis. [Course page](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs120/)
nodes.test: For each week, find the atlas topic that covers it, read one required paper past its introduction, and write down one claim it establishes and one it does not; then check whether the topic's boundary note agrees.

nodes.name: Concrete & unsolved problems in AI safety
nodes.authors: Dario Amodei et al. · Dan Hendrycks et al.
nodes.text: Two problem lists that shaped the field's agenda. Amodei et al. name five accident risks: side effects, reward hacking, scalable supervision, safe exploration and distributional shift. Hendrycks et al. group open work into robustness, monitoring, alignment and systemic safety.
nodes.handle: Amodei et al. sort problems by where they come from: the wrong objective (side effects, reward hacking), an objective too expensive to check often (scalable supervision), or bad behaviour while learning (safe exploration, distributional shift) ([Amodei et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.06565)). Hendrycks et al. sort by what to do about hazards: withstand them, identify them, reduce the model's own hazards, or reduce systemic ones ([Hendrycks et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.13916)).
nodes.boundary: These are research agendas, not results: they name and motivate problems with small illustrative examples. Neither list is complete, and neither estimates how often each failure occurs in deployed systems. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.06565)
nodes.test: Take a published failure or incident, classify it under both taxonomies, and note where the two disagree or where it fits neither.

nodes.name: Safety as a system property: risk taxonomies & sociotechnical framing
nodes.authors: Laura Weidinger et al. · Arvind Narayanan · Sayash Kapoor · Roel Dobbe et al.
nodes.text: Many harms depend on who uses a model, for what, and inside which institution, so safety cannot be read off the model alone. Risk taxonomies map harms from discrimination to misuse; sociotechnical work treats choosing objectives and trade-offs as part of the safety problem.
nodes.handle: Weidinger et al. organize language-model risks into six areas, from discrimination, exclusion and toxicity through misinformation and malicious use to human–computer interaction and environmental and socioeconomic harms ([Weidinger et al.](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3531146.3533088)). Narayanan and Kapoor argue that whether an output is harmful often depends on context the model cannot see, so defences against misuse belong mainly outside the model ([Narayanan and Kapoor](https://www.normaltech.ai/p/ai-safety-is-not-a-model-property)). Dobbe et al. treat the vague, contested choices made while specifying a system as safety decisions in their own right ([Dobbe et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.11022)).
nodes.boundary: These are taxonomies and arguments, not measurements: they do not rank how often each harm occurs, and saying safety is not only a model property does not make model-level work useless. [Scope](https://www.normaltech.ai/p/ai-safety-is-not-a-model-property)
nodes.test: Pick one capability, such as writing persuasive text, and list which of its harms a model-level refusal could prevent and which need controls in the product, the institution or the law.

nodes.name: Constitutional AI & AI feedback (RLAIF)
nodes.authors: Yuntao Bai et al. · Harrison Lee et al.
nodes.text: Train a harmless assistant from a written list of principles instead of human harm labels: the model critiques and revises its own answers, then a model judges pairs of answers to train the reward model used for RL from AI feedback.
nodes.handle: In the supervised phase the model critiques and revises its own responses against the principles; in the RL phase AI preference labels train the preference model, giving a harmless but non-evasive assistant with far fewer human labels ([Bai et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.08073)). Across summarization and helpful and harmless dialogue, RLAIF performed comparably to RLHF ([Lee et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.00267)).
nodes.boundary: Human judgment does not disappear: it moves into choosing the principles and the feedback model, whose errors and biases are inherited. Comparable scores on the reported tasks do not show that AI feedback stays reliable on tasks humans cannot check. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.08073)
nodes.test: Train with two different constitutions on the same data and measure which behaviours change; have humans and the AI labeler rate the same held-out pairs and report where they disagree.

nodes.name: Social choice & pluralistic alignment
nodes.authors: Taylor Sorensen et al. · Tan Zhi-Xuan et al. · Hannah Rose Kirk et al.
nodes.text: Aligning to “human preferences” hides an aggregation problem: people disagree, so some rule for combining their judgments has to be chosen. Social choice theory studies such rules; pluralistic alignment asks models to represent, or be steerable to, a range of views.
nodes.handle: Sorensen et al. define Overton, steerable and distributionally pluralistic models and report evidence that standard alignment procedures may reduce distributional pluralism ([Sorensen et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.05070)). Zhi-Xuan et al. argue that preferences miss much of what values mean and propose aligning to role-appropriate standards agreed by stakeholders ([Zhi-Xuan et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.16984)). The PRISM dataset ties feedback to the demographics and stated values of participants from many countries ([Kirk et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16019)).
nodes.boundary: Classical impossibility results, Arrow's theorem among them, show that no ranked voting rule meets a small set of appealing conditions at once, so a choice is unavoidable. These papers offer frameworks and data, not a settled rule, and pluralism benchmarks are early. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.05070)
nodes.test: Fit one reward model to pooled annotators and one per annotator group, then measure how often the pooled model's preferred answer is rejected by a majority of some group on held-out prompts.

nodes.name: Neural-network verification & validation
nodes.authors: Changliu Liu et al. · Chuyue Sun et al.
