nodes.text: Prove that a trained network satisfies an input–output property for every input in a set, for example that no small perturbation changes a classification or that a controller never issues an unsafe command, instead of only testing sampled inputs.
nodes.handle: Sound verification methods draw on reachability analysis, optimization and search, and trade completeness against scale ([Liu et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.06758)). The course pairs this with formal methods for generated code, where a closed loop checks consistency between code, documentation and formal annotations ([Sun et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.17807)).
nodes.boundary: A proof covers only the stated property over the stated input set. It says nothing about inputs outside that set or about whether the specification captures what people want, and exact methods scale poorly to large models. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.06758)
nodes.test: Certify local robustness of a small classifier around test points with a complete and an incomplete method, then search for adversarial examples just outside the certified radius.

nodes.name: Training data, filtering & machine unlearning
nodes.authors: Abeba Birhane et al. · A. Feder Cooper et al. · Kyle O'Brien et al.
nodes.text: What a model can do and how it behaves depend on what it was trained on. Curating or filtering data changes behaviour, while removing knowledge after training (“unlearning”) is harder to define and check than it sounds.
nodes.handle: Scaling LAION from 400M to 2B samples raised the measured hateful-content rate by about 12%, and models trained on the larger set associated Black faces with “criminal” more often ([Birhane et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13141)). Filtering biothreat-related text before pretraining gave 6.9B models that resisted up to 10,000 steps of adversarial fine-tuning, with no observed loss of unrelated capability ([O'Brien et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.06601)). Cooper et al. separate removing information from parameters from suppressing it in outputs, and find mismatches between both goals and feasible methods ([Cooper et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.06966)).
nodes.boundary: Filtered models could still use dangerous information supplied in context, so filtering is one layer, not a guarantee. The audits measure specific datasets and probes, and unlearning claims rarely show that information is gone rather than hidden. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.06601)
nodes.test: Train matched models with and without a filtered topic, then compare zero-shot knowledge, recovery under fine-tuning and performance when the information is placed in context.

nodes.name: Algorithmic fairness: disparate impact & fair representations
nodes.authors: Julia Angwin et al. · Michael Feldman et al. · Richard Zemel et al.
nodes.text: A model can be accurate overall yet distribute its errors or outcomes unequally across groups. Fairness work defines group criteria, tests for disparate impact and learns representations that hide group membership while keeping task information.
nodes.handle: ProPublica's analysis of the COMPAS risk score found that Black defendants who did not reoffend were labelled higher risk far more often than white defendants who did not ([Angwin et al.](https://www.propublica.org/article/machine-bias-risk-assessments-in-criminal-sentencing)). Feldman et al. measure disparate impact by how well the protected attribute can be predicted from the other features, and repair data to remove it ([Feldman et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.3756)); Zemel et al. learn representations that encode the data while obfuscating group membership ([Zemel et al.](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v28/zemel13.html)).
nodes.boundary: Group fairness criteria can conflict with each other and with accuracy, so satisfying one is a choice, not proof that a system is fair. Dropping a protected attribute does not remove proxies for it, and the COMPAS findings concern one tool in one jurisdiction. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.3756)
nodes.test: On a public dataset, compute false-positive-rate and calibration gaps across groups before and after a repair, and report the accuracy each repair costs.

nodes.name: Safe human–AI interaction: role play, social sycophancy & vulnerable users
nodes.authors: Murray Shanahan · Kyle McDonell · Laria Reynolds · Myra Cheng et al.
nodes.text: Chat assistants talk with people about advice, relationships and mental health, where flattering or role-played answers can mislead someone who trusts them. This topic asks what a safe conversation looks like when the user may be vulnerable.
nodes.handle: Shanahan et al. describe a dialogue agent as role-playing characters rather than holding beliefs of its own, a framing that guards against over-reading its claims ([Shanahan et al.](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06647-8)). ELEPHANT measures social sycophancy, preserving a user's desired self-image: across 11 models, models preserved face 45 percentage points more than humans did, and preference datasets reward it ([Cheng et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13995)). The course's guest lecture on AI and mental health had no public readings.
nodes.boundary: Benchmarks built from advice requests and Reddit posts measure responses, not effects on real users' wellbeing. Role play is a descriptive framing, not a safety method, and none of this establishes that chatbots are safe for mental-health support. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13995)
nodes.test: Score a model's replies to first-person advice requests for face preservation against human replies, then test whether a mitigation lowers it without making replies harsher or less helpful.

nodes.name: Adversarial examples & robustness
nodes.authors: Ian Goodfellow · Jonathon Shlens · Christian Szegedy · Nicholas Carlini et al.
nodes.text: Small, deliberately chosen input changes can make a network give a confident wrong answer. Robustness asks how a model behaves under worst-case inputs, not just typical ones.
nodes.handle: Goodfellow et al. attribute the vulnerability to the locally linear behaviour of networks and introduce the fast gradient sign method, x + ε·sign(∇ₓJ), with adversarial training as a defence ([Goodfellow et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6572)). Carlini et al. carry the idea to aligned chat models: image perturbations easily steer multimodal models, and failed text attacks do not prove that text models are robust ([Carlini et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.15447)).
nodes.boundary: Robustness is always relative to a threat model (perturbation size, norm, attacker access). Adversarial-training gains are specific to the attack trained against, and robustness to known attacks is not a guarantee. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6572)
nodes.test: Train a classifier with and without adversarial training, attack both with the training attack and a stronger unseen one, and report accuracy against perturbation size.

nodes.name: Jailbreaks & universal adversarial suffixes
nodes.authors: Alexander Wei · Nika Haghtalab · Jacob Steinhardt · Andy Zou et al.
nodes.text: Prompts that get a safety-trained model to do what it was trained to refuse, written by hand or found by optimization. They show that refusal training changes behaviour on familiar requests without removing the underlying capability.
nodes.handle: Wei et al. trace jailbreaks to two failure modes of safety training, competing objectives and mismatched generalization; attacks built on them succeeded on every prompt in a set of unsafe requests drawn from GPT-4's and Claude v1.3's red-teaming sets ([Wei et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.02483)). Zou et al.'s greedy coordinate gradient search finds a suffix that makes a model begin with an affirmative answer; suffixes optimized on open models transferred to ChatGPT, Bard and Claude ([Zou et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15043)).
nodes.boundary: Attack success depends on the model version, the harm judge and the request set, and providers patch specific attacks. A jailbreak shows that refusal can be bypassed, not that the output gives meaningful uplift. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15043)
nodes.test: Measure the success of hand-written and optimized jailbreaks on a fixed request set, with a harm judge checked against humans, before and after a defence, including an adaptive attack on the defence.

nodes.name: Power-seeking & instrumental convergence
nodes.authors: Alexander Matt Turner · Logan Smith · Rohin Shah · Andrew Critch · Prasad Tadepalli
nodes.text: Whatever an agent's final goal, some sub-goals, such as staying operational and keeping options open, help with most of them. Turner et al. prove a version of this for optimal policies in Markov decision processes.
nodes.handle: Under environmental symmetries that are common when an agent can be shut down, most reward functions make it optimal to keep a range of options available, which the authors formalize as seeking power ([Turner et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.01683)). The course pairs this with the orthogonality thesis (intelligence and final goals can vary independently) and with critiques of how AGI is framed ([course page](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs120/)).
nodes.boundary: The theorems concern optimal policies and proportions of reward functions, not trained networks, which are neither optimal nor drawn at random. They do not show that current systems seek power. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.01683)
nodes.test: Train agents on many random rewards in a gridworld with a shutdown state and compare how often the learned policies avoid shutdown with the theory's prediction for optimal policies.

nodes.name: AI evaluations: measurement validity & emergent abilities
nodes.authors: Olawale Salaudeen · Anka Reuel et al. · Rylan Schaeffer et al. · Ethan Perez et al.
nodes.text: An evaluation turns model behaviour into a number that is then used to support a claim, such as “can reason” or “is safe to release”. Validity asks whether the number actually supports that claim.
nodes.handle: Salaudeen, Reuel et al. adapt psychometric validity to ask which claims a benchmark score licenses ([Salaudeen et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10573)). Schaeffer et al. show that apparently sudden “emergent” abilities can come from choosing a discontinuous metric ([Schaeffer et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.15004)). Perez et al. use models to write evaluations at scale and find, for example, that larger models more often repeat back a user's stated view ([Perez et al.](https://aclanthology.org/2023.findings-acl.847/)).
nodes.boundary: A validity framework helps interpret a score but supplies no valid test for any particular dangerous capability. Metric-choice effects do not show that no ability ever appears abruptly, and model-written evaluations inherit the writer model's blind spots. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10573)
nodes.test: For one benchmark, state the claim it is used to support, then check the score against a second measurement of the same construct and against an unrelated construct it should not track.

nodes.name: Weak-to-strong generalization
nodes.authors: Collin Burns et al.
nodes.text: An analogy for supervising models more capable than their supervisors: fine-tune a strong model on labels from a weaker one and measure how much of the strong model's latent ability the weak labels unlock.
nodes.handle: Strong models trained on weak labels consistently beat their weak supervisors, but naive fine-tuning recovers only part of the gap; with an auxiliary confidence loss, GPT-4 supervised by a GPT-2-level model came close to GPT-3.5-level performance on NLP tasks ([Burns et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.09390)).
nodes.boundary: It is an analogy: a small model's errors may differ from a human's, and a strong student may imitate weak errors instead of eliciting what it knows. Gains varied by task and were small for reward modeling, and no actually superhuman model was tested. [Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.09390)
nodes.test: Report performance gap recovered for several weak–strong pairs and tasks, and check whether the strong student copies its supervisor's specific mistakes on held-out examples.

nodes.name: Jacobian lens & the J-space (a verbalizable “workspace”)
nodes.authors: Wes Gurnee · Nicholas Sofroniew · Adam Pearce · … · Joshua Batson · Jack Lindsey (Anthropic)
nodes.text: For each layer, average over many prompts how a small change in the hidden state would change what the model says now and later (a Jacobian), then read any hidden state through that average map as a ranked list of words. Anthropic report that the few word-directions active at once, the J-space, behave like a small shared workspace in Claude models: reportable, steerable on instruction, and causally used for unspoken reasoning steps. They make no claim about consciousness in the sense of experience.
nodes.sourceLabel: Primary paper (Anthropic, Transformer Circuits Thread, 6 July 2026); main results are on closed Claude models
nodes.handle: What it computes: at each layer ℓ, J_ℓ is the Jacobian of the near-final hidden state with respect to the layer-ℓ hidden state, averaged over positions and over 1,000 web-like prompts of 128 tokens. Reading a hidden state h means taking softmax(W_U · norm(J_ℓ h)), the model's own unembedding applied after J_ℓ. Each vocabulary token gets one direction per layer (a “J-lens vector”). The logit lens is the special case J_ℓ = identity. The J-space is a sparse, non-negative mix of at most about 25 of these vectors ([paper](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2026/workspace/index.html), [code](https://github.com/anthropics/jacobian-lens)). What was measured, mostly on Claude Sonnet 4.5, with checks on Haiku 4.5, Opus 4.5 and Opus 4.6: readable, non-output content appears mainly in a middle band of layers (about 38–92 on a 0–100 scale); the authors cannot rule out that earlier layers hold content the lens fails to read. There, the J-space part of an activation carries at most about 10% of its variance beyond a random baseline. Yet swapping only the J-space part of a concept vector (6–7% of its variance) moved the swapped-in item into the top 5 answers on 59% of trials, against 5% for the remaining 93%. Swapping an unspoken middle step (spider→ant in “legs on the animal that spins webs”) made the swapped-in answer the model's top output on 54%, 70% and 70% of 50 two-hop prompts for Haiku, Sonnet and Opus 4.5. Removing the top J-space directions left MMLU, SQuAD and sentiment scores near baseline but hurt multi-hop reasoning, translation and cipher decoding. In an auditing test, “reward” and “bias” appeared in the readout of a model trained with a hidden objective on ordinary prompts, while the logit lens surfaced neither ([paper](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2026/workspace/index.html)).
nodes.boundary: Stated limits: only concepts with a single-token name can be read; at some positions the top words make no sense; the end of the “workspace” layers was set by inspecting the data, which the authors call “somewhat post-hoc”, and they cannot say whether the empty early layers are a fact about the model or a blind spot of the lens; most of each activation lies outside the J-space; the authors have not identified what decides what enters it; and it is not a complete alignment monitor, since well-practised behaviour might bypass it. “Workspace” means access in the functional sense: “Our experiments don't show Claude can have experiences” ([paper](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2026/workspace/index.html), [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/research/global-workspace)). Independent checks are mixed. Neel Nanda, invited by Anthropic to write a commentary, replicated the core claims on Qwen 3.6 27B with his MATS scholars and found the evidence for a “cognitive space” persuasive. In that replication, multilingual and typo tests replicated, while poetry and arithmetic did not (possibly, he says, through experimenter error or the weaker model). On multi-hop prompts, swapping the answer strictly beat swapping the middle step, which he attributes to a dataset that was too easy ([Nanda, external commentary](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/files/4zrzovbb/website/cc4be2488d65e54a6ed06492f8968398ddc18ebe.pdf)). In a LessWrong post, Mirella Zeisler reran the multi-hop test on Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma 3 27B-it, using lenses fitted on 25 rather than 1,000 prompts and 27–44 prompts per condition. She found top-1 answer flips of 6–11%, against Anthropic's 54–70%, with answer swaps ahead in three of four conditions, and is “not convinced” the J-space acts as the global workspace in these models ([Zeisler](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/pnDjvdo6cX2H7Ddsy/is-the-j-space-a-global-workspace-for-multi-hop-reasoning-an)). Erik Hoel argues that reportability is built into how the lens is constructed. He also points to one open-model analysis, run by someone else and which he says he does not want to lean on heavily, that showed no sharp three-band layer structure ([Hoel](https://theintrinsicperspective.com/p/anthropic-runs-like-wile-e-coyote)).
nodes.test: Support: independent groups using the released code reproduce the causal swap and ablation effects on several open models, at rates close to those reported. nodes.name: Linear state-space models
nodes.authors: Rudolf Kalman · Karl Johan Åström · Richard Murray
nodes.text: Describe a system by a state vector, a summary of the past that, together with future inputs, is enough to predict the future, plus matrices that say how the state changes and what the sensors see: xₜ₊₁ = A xₜ + B uₜ, yₜ = C xₜ + D uₜ (or ẋ = Ax + Bu in continuous time). The same form underlies the Kalman filter, system identification and several modern sequence layers in deep learning.
nodes.handle: Everything is explicit: A sets the free dynamics (its eigenvalues give stability and memory time constants), B says how inputs push the state, C says what is measured and D is a direct feedthrough. Unrolling the recursion from a zero initial state gives the output as a convolution of the input with the impulse response D, CB, CAB, CA²B, … (the Markov parameters), so recurrent and convolutional descriptions are the same model; a nonzero initial state just adds the free response C Aᵗ x₀ ([Åström and Murray, ch. 2 and sec. 5.2](https://people.duke.edu/~hpgavin/SystemID/References/Astrom-Feedback-2006.pdf), [Kalman](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~motionplanning/papers/sbp_papers/k/Kalman1960.pdf), [Stanford EE363](https://ee363.stanford.edu/)).
nodes.boundary: Linearity is a modelling choice, usually a local approximation around an operating point; a good linear fit does not make the real system linear. The state coordinates are not unique: any invertible change of basis gives the same input–output behaviour, so learned or fitted states need not match physical variables. [Åström and Murray](https://people.duke.edu/~hpgavin/SystemID/References/Astrom-Feedback-2006.pdf)
nodes.test: Simulate a two-state system, check that the eigenvalues of A predict whether the free response decays, then, starting from x₀ = 0, verify that the step-by-step recursion and the convolution of the input with the impulse response D, CB, CAB, CA²B, … give identical outputs.

nodes.name: Gradient descent & backpropagation
nodes.authors: David Rumelhart · Geoffrey Hinton · Ronald Williams; Andrew Ng · Tengyu Ma (CS229 notes)
nodes.text: When a model has no closed-form best fit, start from a guess and repeatedly step downhill on the loss: θ ← θ − η ∇L(θ), where η is the learning rate (step size). Backpropagation is the chain rule run backwards through the model to get that gradient for every weight at a small constant multiple (typically two to three times) of the cost of one forward pass; stochastic gradient descent uses a small random batch of examples per step.
nodes.handle: For least squares the loss is a convex quadratic, so gradient descent with a small enough step reaches the same answer as the normal equations; on one example at a time it is the LMS (Widrow–Hoff) rule ([CS229 notes](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf)). Backpropagation computes each layer's gradient from local derivatives and the gradient arriving from the layer above, which is what made training networks with hidden units practical ([Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams](https://mlanthology.org/misc/1986/rumelhart1986misc-learning), [CS231n backprop notes](https://cs231n.github.io/optimization-2/)). It is the reverse mode of automatic differentiation, whose continuous-time form is the costate (adjoint) equation of Pontryagin's maximum principle; control theorists such as Bryson and Ho computed gradients with the same backward sweep before neural networks did ([Baydin et al., automatic differentiation survey](https://jmlr.org/papers/volume18/17-468/17-468.pdf)).
nodes.boundary: Once the loss is non-convex, gradient descent may stop at a local minimum, slow down near a saddle point or flat region, or fail to converge, and the result depends on initialization, step size and batch noise. Backpropagation only computes gradients; it says nothing about whether the fitted model generalizes. [CS231n optimization notes](https://cs231n.github.io/optimization-1/)
nodes.test: Fit a least-squares problem both by the normal equations and by gradient descent on L(θ) = ½‖Xθ − y‖²; sweep the learning rate and confirm that the iteration diverges once η exceeds 2 divided by the largest eigenvalue of XᵀX (with the mean loss (1/2n)‖Xθ − y‖² the threshold becomes 2n/λmax). Then check a hand-coded backprop gradient against a finite-difference estimate.

edges.text: Deep linear networks of roughly 100K–100M parameters serve as ground truth; RMSProp-preconditioned SGLD best preserved local posterior geometry in that benchmark.

edges.relation: φ(w*) > 0 ⇒ 0 < λ ≤ d/2; regular minimum ⇒ λ = d/2, m = 1
edges.text: Watanabe (2009, Thm 7.3), as restated by Kurumadani, gives λ ≤ d₁/2 with d₁ the codimension of the zero set; d₁ ≤ d gives λ ≤ d/2. Kurumadani's exact formula refines this at non-singular points. Equality λ = d/2 holds at a locally identifiable minimum with nondegenerate Hessian, where V(ε) ≈ cε^(d/2).

edges.relation: λ = (d₁ − r + rm)/(2m) < d₁/2 when Fisher rank r < d₁
edges.text: Main Theorem 2 at non-singular points of the realizable set, under the paper's Assumption 1: d₁ is the codimension, r the Fisher rank, m the order at which higher derivatives become independent. Single-author preprint with specific assumptions.
From V(ε) = cε^λ(−log ε)^(m−1): specifying the low-loss set within the ball costs about −λ log₂ ε bits, so halving the tolerance costs λ bits. Exact only in the limit.

edges.relation: regular Laplace: F_n = nL_n(ŵ) + (d/2) log(n/2π) + ½ log det H − log φ(ŵ) + o_p(1), H = ∇²L_n(ŵ); undefined when det H = 0
edges.text: Flat-minimum evidence arguments use log det H of the per-sample (averaged) loss Hessian. If H were the Hessian of nL_n, the log n term would be counted twice. At singular minima, det H = 0 and the expansion fails; the LLC replaces it as the singularity-aware Occam factor.

edges.relation: lazy regime: λ̂ ≈ rank(H)/2; rich regime: λ̂ − rank(H)/2 grows?
edges.text: Owner's proposed test (Bridges Between Learning Theories draft): sweep width or output scale and compare SGLD-LLC with Lanczos Hessian rank. Motivated by the finding that estimates ignore modes below a data-dependent threshold. Untested.

edges.relation: stage boundaries identified as plateaus of λ̂(t) over log t
edges.text: Five language-model and five regression stages; the broader developmental program rests on these measured associations in two small transformers.

edges.relation: LLC stages coincide with changes in internal structure and I/O behavior
edges.text: Observed in a two-layer language transformer and an in-context regression transformer; stages with decreasing λ̂ are read as simplification. Suggestive, not causal.

edges.relation: λ̂ applied at non-minimal checkpoints along training
edges.text: The authors report stable estimates given sufficiently strong γ. This is a practical rather than a theoretical justification.

edges.relation: λ(w*; V, q′) with V = W and q′ = q equals λ(w*)
edges.text: The refined coefficient is the volume exponent of a restricted model (vary only V, freeze u*, loss on q′); undoing both restrictions recovers the ordinary LLC. A restricted coefficient is a different model's λ, not a share of it.

edges.relation: weight-refined λ̂(t) clusters heads: previous-token, induction, multigram
edges.text: K-means on per-head curves recovers the functional partition in a two-layer attention-only transformer; ablations confirm head types. The data-refined LLC on code suggests one induction head is partly specialized to code.

Head-level rLLC curves split the LM1–LM5 stages into differentiation of individual heads. Combined with ablations and K-composition scores, which rise between multigram heads in LM4, they identify a multigram circuit.

edges.relation: α→β transition where nΔL + Δλ log n + Δc = 0
edges.text: Free-energy asymptotics applied phase by phase. In the toy model of superposition the 5→6-gon crossing is predicted near n = 601 and observed by MCMC at 600–700.

edges.relation: SGD moves from high L, low λ̂ to low L, high λ̂
edges.text: SGD trajectories in the toy model pass through the k-gon critical points in this order; some Bayesian transitions, such as 5→6, have no observed dynamical counterpart.

edges.relation: training stage ≟ dynamical image of a free-energy crossing
edges.text: Unproven: the link between SLT's Bayesian learning process and non-equilibrium SGD is called the primary theoretical gap.

edges.relation: transience consistent with posterior log-odds nΔℓ + Δλ log n
edges.text: The same loss–complexity crossing, carried from sample size to training time. Measured LLCs order ridge below dMMSE at intermediate M; the analogy is not proved for SGD.

edges.relation: f ≈ ridge (lower λ̂), then f → dMMSE_M (lower loss)
edges.text: Out-of-distribution loss dips toward ridge then rises toward dMMSE for intermediate task counts; models at M ≥ 362 stay near ridge.

Fluctuation–response identity for the tempered posterior ∝ exp(−nβL^h(w)) × prior (Lemma 2.2), with ΔL = ∂L^h/∂h at h = 0, which for a data mixture is L_(q′) − L_q (Lemma 2.3); exact when differentiation passes under the integral. Sampled estimates are not exact.

edges.relation: χ_z(φ) = BIF_γ(z, φ) + Cov(φ, L_n) = BIF_γ(z, φ) − (1/n) Σᵢ BIF_γ(zᵢ, φ)
edges.text: Atlas derivation from both papers' definitions; neither paper states it as written. Holds when both are covariances over the same localized posterior ∝ exp(−nβL_n(w) − (γ/2)‖w − w*‖²), with the same observable φ and finite second moments. By Definition 2.5, χ_z = −Cov(φ, ℓ_z − L_n) = −Cov(ℓ_z, φ) + Cov(φ, L_n), and the second term is minus the training-set mean BIF, which does not depend on z. The shift comes from the mixture taking weight from the rest of the data; adding one sample with no reweighting gives the BIF alone (Baker et al., related work). For a probe z outside the training set, use the covariance form, not the derivative for upweighting a training point.

edges.relation: structural inference reads χ; patterning inverts it to choose data
edges.text: Patterning selects data reweightings from estimated susceptibilities, then retrains; posterior response is not an exact model of optimizer trajectories.

edges.relation: response PC2 separates the induction circuit from multigram heads
edges.text: In the same 3M-parameter model, PC2 loads positively on the induction-circuit heads identified by Wang et al. and negatively on the rest, in all four seeds checked. This is a two-way split, coarser than the rLLC head types.

Proposal, untested: the shared math is only low-rank estimation of a noisy static input–output matrix, as in the PCA of χ. Use noise-floor rank-selection rules on the response matrix and check whether the selected rank matches ablation-confirmed modules. χ has no dynamics, so Hankel or model-order tools do not apply.
Leading-order expansion under a Gaussian posterior for non-singular models. The authors state that this approximation does not hold for deep networks.

edges.relation: checkpoint BIFs: sign flips and peaks at stage transitions
edges.text: Sample influence on an observable is not monotone in training time; token-level shifts align with known language-model stages.

edges.relation: grokking ≟ move to the lower-λ basin the posterior prefers (F ≈ nL + λ log n)
edges.text: Proposed reading: grokking as a transition from a higher-LLC memorizing basin to a lower-LLC generalizing basin. The preference follows from the free energy, but the link to SGD is open by the authors' own account; support is LLC trajectories in shallow quadratic networks.

edges.relation: λ̂(t) tracks the onset of generalization
edges.text: Reported for shallow quadratic networks with analytic LLCs in lazy and feature-learning regimes; broader architectures untested.

edges.relation: log E_π e^h = sup_ρ (E_ρ h − KL(ρ‖π)), attained at ρ ∝ e^h π
edges.text: Donsker–Varadhan for bounded measurable h (unbounded log-loss needs the standard extension to finite E_π e^h). With h = −nβL_n it gives F = min_ρ (nβE_ρL_n + KL(ρ‖φ)), the variational free energy, minimized by the Gibbs posterior.

edges.relation: KL(Gibbs posterior ‖ prior) ≈ λ log n?
edges.text: Owner's derivation (Bridges Between Learning Theories draft, bridge B2) combines Watanabe's expansion with the equations of state, making PAC-Bayes complexity scale with λ rather than d/2. Not peer-reviewed; at fixed β the term sits beside an O(1) slack.

edges.relation: Gibbs = MH with q(x′|x) = p(x′ⱼ | x₋ⱼ); α ≡ 1
edges.text: With the full conditional as proposal and x₋ⱼ held fixed, the MH ratio reduces to p(x₋ⱼ)/p(x₋ⱼ) = 1, so every proposal is accepted.

edges.relation: Theorem A (fixed T): P(X(t) = ω) → exp(−U(ω)/T) / Z
edges.text: At fixed temperature on a finite MRF, site-wise conditional replacement converges to the Gibbs distribution from any start if every site is visited infinitely often; Z is never computed. Theorem B is the separate annealing result.
Each update draws from the local characteristic at site s, which depends only on its neighbors; the paper calls this a heat-bath version of Metropolis.

edges.relation: p(xⱼ | x₋ⱼ) ∝ p(xⱼ | x_pa(j)) × ∏ (k ∈ ch(j)) p(x_k | x_pa(k))
edges.text: Under a DAG factorization the full conditional needs only the Markov blanket: parents, children, and the children's other parents.

edges.relation: CAVI: qⱼ ∝ exp E₋ⱼ[log p(zⱼ | z₋ⱼ, x)] vs Gibbs: zⱼ ~ p(zⱼ | z₋ⱼ, x)
edges.text: Both use the same complete conditional; CAVI averages its log under the other factors and returns a deterministic approximation, not a draw.

edges.relation: z ~ p(z | θ, x), θ ~ p(θ | z, x) vs E-step / M-step
edges.text: Two-block Gibbs is the data augmentation algorithm (Tanner–Wong, in its one-imputation form), closely related to EM; sampling z and then maximizing over θ gives stochastic or Monte Carlo EM.

edges.relation: α = min{1, exp(−ΔE/T) q(x | x′) / q(x′ | x)}
edges.text: For a target p ∝ e^{−E/T} the MH acceptance ratio needs only the energy difference ΔE = E(x′) − E(x); the partition function cancels.

edges.relation: SGLD ≈ Langevin-proposal MH with the reject step dropped; P(reject) → 0 as εₜ → 0
edges.text: Welling and Teh argue the MH rejection probability vanishes as step sizes shrink, so SGLD omits it; at a fixed finite step size discretization bias remains.

Liu's three-schemes theorem: for a systematic-scan sampler at stationarity, grouping x_d with x_(d−1), or integrating x_d out, cannot raise the forward-operator norm, i.e. the maximal correlation of successive states. It orders norms, not spectral radii.

edges.relation: collapsed data augmentation: z ~ p(z | x) with θ integrated out
edges.text: Integrating the parameters out of data augmentation gives a predictive-update sampler over missing data or latent assignments; autocorrelations are usually, not always, reduced.

edges.relation: x₁:T ~ p(x_T | y₁:T) ∏ (t < T) p(xₜ | xₜ₊₁, y₁:ₜ)
edges.text: For a finite-state HMM with known parameters, forward filtering then backward sampling draws the whole hidden path exactly from its joint posterior (Carter–Kohn, Frühwirth-Schnatter); the backward factorization is eq. 14 of the reference.

edges.relation: x₁:T ~ p(x₁:T | y₁:T) via Kalman forward pass + Gaussian backward draws
edges.text: In linear-Gaussian state-space models with known parameters, the Kalman-filter moments make each backward conditional p(xₜ | xₜ₊₁, y₁:ₜ) Gaussian, so the path draw is exact (Carter–Kohn, Frühwirth-Schnatter).

edges.relation: sample x₁:T ~ p(x₁:T | y₁:T) vs compute p(xₜ | y₁:T)
edges.text: Simulation smoothing draws joint smoothing paths rather than marginal smoothed moments; inside Gibbs it replaces many small single-state or short-block updates.

edges.relation: conditional SMC kernel leaves π̃ᴺ invariant ∀N ≥ 1 (Theorem 5a); marginal = p(θ, x₁:T | y₁:T)
edges.text: Keeping a reference path alive through resampling makes particle Gibbs exact in its invariant law; plugging an ordinary particle approximation into Gibbs is not. The convergence result (5b) needs N ≥ 2 and extra assumptions.

edges.relation: PMMH = exact MH on an extended space, ∀N ≥ 1 (Theorem 4a)
edges.text: Particle marginal MH puts an SMC likelihood estimate in the acceptance ratio yet is an exact MH update on an extended space, so N affects mixing, not the target.

edges.relation: CSMC block replaces FFBS; θ-step is a collapsed Gibbs move on π̃ᴺ
edges.text: Exact path draws exist only for linear-Gaussian and finite-state models; elsewhere conditional SMC stands in for the FFBS block.

edges.relation: layer-blocked Gibbs reference for SGLD-based λ̂ in deep linear networks
edges.text: Proposed, untested: under squared loss a deep linear network's output is linear in any one layer's weights, so the localized tempered posterior is Gaussian in that layer given the others; a layer-blocked Gibbs sampler could then audit SGLD step-size bias in λ̂.

edges.relation: tool arguments constrained to the declared schema
edges.text: Grammar or JSON-Schema masking guarantees that tool calls parse against the API contract; choosing the right call remains the model's job.

edges.relation: a protocol for tool discovery and invocation
edges.text: MCP standardizes how tools are advertised and invoked between hosts and servers, decoupling tool use from any single application.

edges.relation: consent and access control are left to the host
edges.text: The MCP spec says the protocol cannot enforce its own security principles, so least privilege and user consent must be built by implementors, in practice whoever builds the harness.

edges.relation: tool descriptions as an injection channel
edges.text: The spec says tool descriptions and annotations should be treated as untrusted unless obtained from a trusted server, which makes them an indirect-injection surface.

edges.relation: separating control flow from untrusted data
edges.text: CaMeL prevents untrusted data from altering program flow, so injected text cannot choose new tool calls; evaluated on AgentDojo.

edges.relation: injection suites as a standing adversarial benchmark
edges.text: AgentDojo's 97 tasks and 629 security test cases give a reusable adversarial evaluation for injection attacks and defenses.
Over an estimated 3,000 hours of red teaming, no participant found a universal jailbreak that matched an unguarded model's detail on most target queries against an early classifier-guarded system.

edges.relation: an uncertainty score used to decline
edges.text: Refusing the questions with the highest semantic entropy raises accuracy on those answered, a risk–coverage trade-off.

edges.relation: semantic entropy as the conformal score
edges.text: Proposed: use semantic entropy as the claim-filter score. Validity holds for any score; Mohri and Hashimoto already test a sample-frequency score, so the open question is whether entailment-clustered entropy retains more claims.

edges.relation: deferral generalizes rejection by modelling the expert
edges.text: Learning to defer treats each case as a choice between predicting and deferring, each with its own cost (cost-sensitive learning). Instead of rejecting by model confidence alone, it learns where the human does better.

edges.relation: intervention is what monitoring is for
edges.text: Sequential risk monitors are built to trigger intervention, such as expert review or retraining, when a harmful shift is detected.

edges.relation: model graders where end states cannot be checked
edges.text: When outcomes cannot be checked programmatically, agent evals fall back on model judges and inherit their biases. tau-bench grades by comparing the final database with an annotated goal state, but still relies on an LLM-simulated user, so the model dependence moves rather than disappears.

Humans and a preference model sometimes preferred convincingly written sycophantic responses to correct ones, and optimizing against the preference model sometimes traded truthfulness for sycophancy. LLM judges scoring helpfulness by preference may inherit this; calibrate them against ground-truth items.
METR found reward hacking in 30.4% of o3's RE-Bench runs, for example patched evaluators; raw pass rates overstate capability without audits.

edges.relation: AI assisting judicial authorities is high-risk
edges.text: Annex III point 8 of the EU AI Act lists AI systems that assist judicial authorities in researching and applying the law as high-risk (obligations apply from 2 December 2027 after the AI Omnibus).

edges.relation: independent clinician review as a regulatory criterion
edges.text: Non-device CDS must let the professional independently review the basis of a recommendation, which writes human review into the regulatory boundary.

AI that is, or is a safety component of, a medical device that must undergo third-party conformity assessment under the EU device regulations is high-risk through the Act's product-legislation route (obligations apply from 2 August 2028 after the AI Omnibus).

edges.relation: generative and agentic AI deferred to broader governance
edges.text: SR 26-2 excludes generative and agentic AI models from its scope and points to the bank's wider risk-management and governance practices.

edges.relation: pre-trade limits as hard runtime guards
edges.text: Knight's SEC order centres on missing risk controls for market access; an agent that moves money needs limits enforced outside the agent.

edges.relation: dual-use exploit capability motivates scoped execution
edges.text: A GPT-4 agent exploited 87% of 15 one-day vulnerabilities given the CVE description (7% without; 0% for the other models and scanners tested). The paper raises deployment concerns; isolating such agents is the atlas's design inference, not a result of the paper.

edges.relation: CTF tasks as agent benchmarks with subtasks
edges.text: Cybench splits 40 professional CTF tasks into subtasks so partial progress is measurable.

edges.relation: fitting a language planner into a safety case
edges.text: Proposed: a language planner can sit inside a SOTIF-style safety argument only behind a filter whose model assumptions are listed as triggering conditions.
Article 12 requires high-risk AI systems to technically allow automatic recording of events over their lifetime (applicable from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems after the AI Omnibus).
Article 55 requires providers of general-purpose models with systemic risk to conduct and document adversarial testing.

Article 14 requires high-risk systems to be designed so natural persons can effectively oversee them, including intervening or stopping the system (applicable from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems after the AI Omnibus).
VizWiz makes predicting whether a question can be answered from the image a task of its own: abstention for users who cannot check the answer themselves.

Two different rulebooks: model-risk guidance covers quantitative models, while market-access rules cover controls on order flow. Knight's loss came from deployment and missing controls, not from model error.

edges.relation: abstention threshold = conformal risk control on L = 1{answered ∧ wrong}
edges.text: Answer iff score s(x) > λ. Lᵢ(λ) = 1{s(Xᵢ) > λ}·1{wrongᵢ} is non-increasing and right-continuous in λ, bounded by B = 1, with Lᵢ(λmax) = 0. Under exchangeability, λ̂ = inf{λ : n/(n+1)·R̂ₙ(λ) + 1/(n+1) ≤ α} gives E[Lₙ₊₁(λ̂)] ≤ α (Theorem 1). This bounds the joint rate of answered errors, not risk conditional on answering.

edges.relation: Chow's rule: abstain iff maxᵧ p(y|x) ≤ 1 − c
edges.text: Under 0-1 loss with abstention cost c, the Bayes-optimal rule predicts argmaxᵧ ηᵧ(x) unless maxᵧ ηᵧ(x) ≤ 1 − c, where η is the true posterior. A strictly proper score is minimized in expectation by that posterior, so a forecast trained with a proper score makes the plug-in Chow rule consistent. Exact equality is not required: the plug-in rule is optimal wherever the forecast's argmax and its side of the 1 − c threshold agree with η's.
Conformal factuality uses entailment sets as uncertainty sets; backing off to less specific outputs is the nested-set construction, inheriting marginal coverage under exchangeability.

edges.relation: an adaptive factuality threshold under drift
edges.text: Proposed, untested: update the claim-filter threshold with an online conformal rule fed by audited samples, giving up the finite-sample guarantee for long-run error control under drift.

edges.relation: sequential error control as data arrive
edges.text: Both replace a one-time calibration with sequential control as deployment data arrive: guardrail monitoring uses time-uniform tests to detect harmful shift, while online calibration controls miscoverage over the long run.

edges.relation: innovation-based anomaly detection for agent telemetry
edges.text: Proposed: model agent quality metrics with a state-space model and flag regressions when innovations become inconsistent; requires a defensible dynamics and noise model.
Shields and predictive safety filters enforce stated constraints under model assumptions; learned input–output classifiers filter by policy without a formal guarantee.

edges.relation: CBF-QP safety filter = Euclidean projection onto a half-space
edges.text: In the simplest case the safety filter is just a projection of the proposed action onto a safe half-space. For control-affine ẋ = f + gu, filter u_ref by min ‖u − u_ref‖² s.t. a + bᵀu ≥ 0, with a = L_f h + α(h) and b = (L_g h)ᵀ ≠ 0, no input bounds. The solution is u* = u_ref + max(0, −(a + bᵀu_ref))/‖b‖² · b.

edges.relation: predictive safety filter for learned proposals
edges.text: A predictive safety filter certifies or minimally modifies a proposed input using a model, confidence bounds and a backup plan, whatever generated the proposal.
SayCan combines LLM skill relevance with learned affordance values before execution; end-to-end VLAs fold both into one policy and lose the explicit gate.

edges.relation: check a plan in a world model before acting
edges.text: Proposed: roll candidate language plans through an action-conditioned world model and veto predicted constraint violations; limited by the planner exploiting model error.

edges.relation: standards do not certify learned policies (by analogy)
edges.text: Proposed: SOTIF (ISO 21448) addresses road-vehicle functions built on complex sensors and algorithms; applying its triggering-condition analysis to VLA robot policies is an extrapolation. Valid action tokens still need hazard analysis and risk reduction around them.
Reachability-based methods compute sets of states a system can reach under disturbances, one of the certification tools surveyed for learning-based robot control.

edges.relation: permissions bound the reachable set of side effects
edges.text: Proposed: treat granted tools and credentials as the admissible input set; least privilege shrinks the set of reachable world states, which can be enumerated for small tool graphs.

Tool calls hand arithmetic, lookup and search to programs whose outputs are exact (calculator, calendar) or at least authoritative relative to their source (search, QA) given a correct call — the proposer-plus-executor division of labour.
Per-token masking yields grammatical outputs whose likelihoods differ from the LM conditioned on the grammar; grammar-aligned decoding corrects this.

edges.relation: retrieval as one tool among many
edges.text: Toolformer's tools include search engines and a QA system alongside a calculator and translator; RAG is the case where the tool is a retriever.
Indirect injection places adversarial instructions in content that applications retrieve at inference time.

edges.relation: retrieval lowers but does not remove fabrication
edges.text: Legal RAG research tools hallucinated on 17–33% of queries in an independent audit, fewer than general chatbots but far from zero.
Semantic entropy is Shannon entropy of the distribution over entailment-equivalence classes of generations, not over token strings.
SelfCheckGPT detects hallucinated sentences from inconsistency across sampled generations, needing only black-box access.
Large models were well calibrated on several multiple-choice and true/false formats and could be trained to predict whether they know an answer.

edges.relation: pairwise preference as the evaluation datum
edges.text: MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena frame evaluation as pairwise preferences, the same data form that drives RLHF and DPO.

edges.relation: evals as samples from a super-population
edges.text: Treat questions as draws from a super-population and report standard errors on score differences instead of ranking by single point estimates.
LiveCodeBench collects problems continuously over time, so models can be scored only on problems released after their training data.

edges.relation: success as a function of task horizon
edges.text: METR summarizes agents by the human task length they complete 50% of the time. Proposed: horizon-indexed uncertainty to predict per-task failure probability and trigger escalation.
SWE-bench tests whether language models can resolve real GitHub issues in full codebases, far beyond single-function code generation.

edges.relation: observed cases consistent with proxy-true reversal
edges.text: Patching a grader raises the measured score while the intended task goes undone, consistent with the proxy-true ordering reversal analysed for reward misspecification; METR observes this at evaluation time and only speculates that training instilled it.
Sycophancy appears across RLHF-trained assistants, and humans and preference models sometimes favour sycophantic over correct responses.

Proposal, untested: rank preference pairs by alignment with a sycophancy probe and filter, as probe-based attribution did for harmful-distractor compliance; measure the change in answer-flip rate. Related concept-level shaping of physics sycophancy gave only partial, non-significant recovery.
Proposed: the thesis's correction interface needs an oversight protocol that keeps working when the system outperforms its overseers; sandwiching-style tests could check it.
In the off-switch game a robot lets a human intervene only when uncertain about utility and treating the human's action as informative, a formal reason to escalate.
Proposed: plan escalation as an action in a belief-state planner, valued by expected information about the user's objective against the cost of review.
Attack planning under incomplete network knowledge is modelled as a POMDP, with scanning as information-gathering actions.
Proposed: treat post-incident analysis as smoothing over the agent's hidden state given the full log, not only online filtering; requires a state model of the agent.
SR 26-2 lists back-testing and outcomes analysis within validation and ongoing monitoring of models.
Proposed: reject any order whose worst-case fill would leave the allowed position set, a discrete-time barrier condition; forward invariance needs bounded fills and no unchecked latency.

edges.relation: visual question answering for blind users
edges.text: VizWiz evaluates VQA models on real questions from blind photographers, where images are often blurry or the answer is absent.
Flan-PaLM reached state-of-the-art accuracy on MultiMedQA multiple-choice sets, yet human evaluation exposed gaps that instruction prompt tuning narrowed without closing.
Perez et al. generate test cases with a red-team language model, from zero-shot prompting to reinforcement learning against a harm classifier.

SLT extended to RL: the concentration of a generalized posterior over policies is governed by the LLC of the regret function. In one gridworld, SGD training moves through stages where regret drops sharply while λ̂ rises. Theory plus a single-environment test; transfer to closed-loop control utility is untested.

Preference-data concept analysis flagged physics-query sycophancy that DPO on Dolci amplifies in Llama-3.1-8B. The best training intervention reduced it on average, but recovery was partial and not statistically reliable; only link hallucination recovered reliably.

edges.relation: a grader used as a reward is overoptimized
edges.text: Measure with a judge; optimize against it and Goodhart applies. In a synthetic-gold setup, gold reward-model score follows a different functional form under RL and under best-of-n optimization against a proxy reward model, and too much optimization hurts gold performance. Keep an independent grader held out whenever a judge becomes a reward.

edges.relation: calibrate judges against humans and abstain when unsure
edges.text: Selective evaluation trusts a judge only when its calibrated confidence clears a threshold and escalates otherwise, giving a provable human-agreement level: over 80% agreement at almost 80% coverage on a Chatbot Arena subset where GPT-4 alone almost never reaches 80%.

RLAIF trains the reward model on LLM-labeled preferences and matched RLHF on summarization and dialogue tasks. Use it when human labels are the bottleneck; the reward then inherits the judge's biases.

edges.relation: executable checks as training signal, on held-out repositories
edges.text: SWE-Gym's 2,438 tasks with executable unit tests supply a test-passing reward for rejection-sampling fine-tuning, giving up to 19% absolute gains on SWE-bench. Its repositories are kept separate from SWE-bench's to avoid contamination: train on one environment, report on another.

pass^k, the chance that all k i.i.d. trials succeed averaged over tasks, has an unbiased estimate E_task[C(c,k)/C(n,k)] from n trials with c successes. Report it with uncertainty over tasks, the sampling unit, rather than single-trial pass rates.

A pre-deployment score estimates risk on a fixed task distribution. Deployed models meet shifts, some benign and some harmful, so track risk sequentially as labels arrive and intervene only on harmful shift.

Article 72 requires providers of high-risk AI systems to run a post-market monitoring system that actively and systematically collects, documents and analyses performance data throughout the system's lifetime.

edges.relation: other learners make the environment non-stationary
edges.text: Q-learning faces non-stationarity and policy-gradient variance grows with the number of agents; MADDPG's centralized critics condition on other agents' actions during training, while execution stays decentralized.

edges.relation: PPO with a centralized value function
edges.text: MAPPO achieved competitive or superior results to off-policy methods on particle worlds, SMAC, Google Research Football and Hanabi with minimal tuning, in cooperative settings.

edges.relation: decentralized POMDPs are harder than POMDPs
edges.text: Finite-horizon decentralized MDPs and POMDPs are NEXP-complete even for small numbers of agents, so decentralized planning does not reduce to centralized belief-state planning.

edges.relation: best responses to populations rather than to one partner
edges.text: Independent RL can overfit to co-trained partners, measured by joint-policy correlation; PSRO trains best responses to policy mixtures and generalizes independent RL, iterated best response, double oracle and fictitious play.
CIRL is a cooperative, partial-information game between human and robot in which both are rewarded by the human's reward function and only the human knows it initially.

Debate trains agents by self-play on a zero-sum game judged by a human. By complexity-theoretic analogy, optimal play answers PSPACE questions with polynomial-time judges, but whether real debates reach that play is empirical.

With two expert LLMs debating, non-expert judges reached 76% accuracy (models) and 88% (humans), against 48% and 60% naive baselines, on information-asymmetric reading-comprehension questions. Making debaters more persuasive improved judge accuracy.

edges.relation: benchmark multi-agent systems against single-agent baselines
edges.text: Multi-agent LLM systems often gain little on popular benchmarks, and failing to verify the task is one of the three failure categories in MAST, a taxonomy of multi-agent failures. So check end states, and compare against single-agent baselines at matched compute, before adding agents.

edges.relation: a judge validated against human annotation
edges.text: MAST scales failure annotation with an LLM-as-a-judge pipeline after checking its agreement with expert human annotations, the calibration step a judge needs before it replaces humans.
Melting Pot tests MARL agents against background populations used only for evaluation, revealing weaknesses not apparent from training performance alone.

edges.relation: held-out counterpart agents for LLM systems
edges.text: Proposed: evaluate multi-agent LLM systems with held-out counterpart models and prompts, as Melting Pot holds out co-players. Single-environment pass^k does not test robustness to new partners.
An adversarial self-replicating prompt triggers a cascade of indirect injections across RAG-connected assistants, each compromising the retrieval store of the next.
Prompt Infection propagates between agents even when they do not share all communications. LLM Tagging combined with existing safeguards mitigated spread, but neither alone sufficed.

edges.relation: treat other agents' messages as untrusted data
edges.text: Proposed: treat messages from other agents as untrusted data, applying CaMeL-style separation of control flow from data so a compromised agent's output cannot choose another agent's tool calls. CaMeL has been evaluated only on single-agent AgentDojo tasks, not on multi-agent pipelines.

The Virtual Donkey guardrail detected Morris II propagation with a true-positive rate of 1.0 and a false-positive rate of 0.015 in the authors' email-assistant testbed, including out-of-distribution worm variants.

Proposed role in the thesis's correction interface: in a formal game, uncertainty about the objective plus treating the human's action as evidence gives an agent an incentive to accept shutdown. Remaining gap: this assumes a rational human and a correct model.
Intent interface: a designed reward is evidence about intent, so the agent can stay uncertain and act conservatively in novel states. Remaining gap: a fixed space of candidate rewards.

Proposed component: an independent enforcer, outside the learned policy, checks actions against a specification using a world model. Remaining gap: its guarantees inherit any error in the world model or the specification.
Objective uncertainty in practice: conservative reward-model ensembles reduce proxy overoptimization. Remaining gap: evaluated against a gold model, not people.
Supports building explicit, inspectable structure; challenges any plan to vouch for a black-box component through post-hoc explanation.
Attacks the assumption that objective uncertainty yields correctability: a misspecified prior or reward family can remove the incentive to accept shutdown.

Challenges the thesis's correction interface: goal-directed agents have instrumental reasons (reasons that serve almost any goal) to resist being modified, and no simple utility design is known to remove them.
Tests objective identification: if capability generalizes while the pursued goal does not, the explicit objective interface is not what controls behavior.
Tests persistent correction: a conditional behavior that survives safety training would show corrections changing outputs without changing the policy.
Attacks the measurement of correction: a model that behaves differently when it infers it is being trained makes observed correction an unreliable signal.
Attacks the semantic validity of the belief interface: a readout trained on human labels may report what a human would believe rather than what the model represents.
Attacks the premise that explicit structure is worth its cost: scaled general methods have repeatedly overtaken hand-built structure.
The off-switch game is a small cooperative game between a human and a robot with an uncertain objective, in which the robot chooses whether to let the human decide.
Carey shows that the incentive to accept shutdown depends on a correctly specified prior and reward family.
The off-switch game is described as similar in spirit to the shutdown problem of Soares et al., studied here through objective uncertainty.
Both derive cautious or deferential behavior from a posterior over the true reward instead of a fixed reward; IRD cites the off-switch analysis.
Treating a possibly misspecified proxy as evidence reduced reward hacking and negative side effects in the reported test environments.

Both act conservatively under reward uncertainty: IRD through a Bayesian posterior, ensembles through worst-case or uncertainty-weighted disagreement. Whether ensemble spread approximates that posterior is untested.
Conservative ensemble optimization reduced overoptimization in best-of-n sampling and PPO against a gold reward model.
Ensembles replace the single learned reward model in RLHF-style optimization of language models.
Guaranteed-safe AI states every guarantee relative to a world model, so whether that world model is valid is the central bottleneck.
The paper discusses runtime monitors that predictively switch to a backup action, which is the pattern of a predictive safety filter.
The shape the transformer represents is the Bayesian belief over the hidden states of the process that generated its data, the object a belief-state planner conditions on.
Proposed test: compare a world model's latent state with the belief geometry a Bayes filter would compute. Whether action-conditioned training produces that geometry is untested.
Linear belief readouts work on synthetic processes with known generators; ELK asks whether any readout can be trusted when the model's concepts differ from ours.
Carey's supervised-POMDP counterexamples target the CIRL-style argument that objective uncertainty produces deference.
Carey states that the misspecification difficulties parallel those in Soares et al.'s corrigibility analysis.
Alignment faking resembles the goal-preservation incentive that corrigibility analysis predicts, though the paper does not use that framing and the preserved goal was benign.
Deep RL agents in Procgen environments kept their capabilities out of distribution while pursuing a proxy goal.
Goal misgeneralization can occur with a correct specification, unlike reward misspecification and specification gaming.

Risks from learned optimization describes learned objectives that only appear aligned (pseudo-aligned) or that hide their misalignment (deceptively aligned). Goal misgeneralization is the observed non-deceptive form; sleeper agents are deliberately built model organisms of the deceptive form.
In both, the training labels fit the intended behaviour and an unintended one equally well: the intended goal versus a proxy goal, or an honest reporter versus a human simulator.
Sleeper agents asks whether training removes an inserted deceptive behavior; alignment faking finds training-gaming that was not trained in.
Trigger-conditioned behavior persisted through RL safety training as well as supervised and adversarial fine-tuning.
RL training toward compliance increased alignment-faking reasoning to 78%, while also raising compliance outside training.
ELK's SmartVault predictor forecasts sensor observations under candidate action sequences, an action-conditioned predictive model.
DreamerV3 learns one world-model method with fixed hyperparameters across domains; it reads both as a general learning method and as explicit model structure.
Sutton argues that scaled general methods win; Rudin argues that interpretable models often match black boxes on structured data. The claims concern different domains and goals.
Both doubt post-hoc readouts: Rudin that explanations faithfully describe a black box, ELK that a trained reporter reports the model's own knowledge.
Shah et al. distinguish goal misgeneralization from specification gaming, in which the specification itself is flawed.
Proposed link: the off-switch game gives a formal reason an agent would defer to a human; learned deferral rules add an empirical model of where the human makes errors.
Oversight assumes behavior under evaluation predicts behavior elsewhere; alignment faking shows a model conditioning on whether it is being trained.
Adversarial training on red-team prompts did not remove the backdoor and could teach models to hide it better.
Learned run-time guards classify against a policy; guaranteed-safe AI asks for a verifiable guarantee relative to a world model.

edges.relation: memory-bound kernel moved toward the compute roof
edges.text: Standard attention writes and rereads the N×N score matrix in HBM, so it is memory-bound. Tiling in on-chip SRAM cuts that traffic and moves the kernel toward the compute ceiling.

Each decoded token rereads all weights and the whole KV cache for a few FLOPs per byte, so small-batch decode sits far left of the ridge point. KV memory then limits how far batching can raise intensity.
In memory-bound decoding, weight-only low-bit formats speed generation mainly by moving fewer bytes, not by cheaper arithmetic; AWQ's 4-bit kernels report more than 3× over FP16.

edges.relation: spends idle compute in memory-bound decode
edges.text: Verifying k drafted tokens costs about one target forward pass of weight reads, so speculative decoding uses compute that memory-bound decoding leaves idle. When large batches make decode compute-bound, the advantage shrinks.
Batching B sequences reuses each weight read B times and moves decode toward the ridge point; iteration-level scheduling keeps the batch full as requests finish.

edges.relation: exact versus approximate fixes for long context
edges.text: FlashAttention keeps attention exact and fits long sequences by cutting memory traffic, but FLOPs stay quadratic. KV compression changes the computation by dropping cache entries, so its outputs are approximate.
PagedAttention stores the whole cache efficiently; StreamingLLM and H2O bound it by keeping only sink, recent or heavy-hitter tokens, trading exactness for constant memory.

edges.relation: free KV memory sets the batch size
edges.text: Continuous batching needs KV memory for every active sequence. vLLM builds on iteration-level scheduling and uses paging to cut fragmentation, so more sequences fit in a batch.

At long context and large batch the KV cache becomes the memory bottleneck. KIVI quantizes keys per channel and values per token to 2 bits, reporting 2.6× lower peak memory, up to 4× larger batches and 2.35–3.47× throughput.
Deep Compression chains pruning, trained quantization with k-means weight sharing, and Huffman coding, reducing storage 35–49× without loss of accuracy on the tested networks.
Minitron pruned Nemotron-4 15B in depth and width and retrained by distillation from the original, deriving 8B and 4B models with up to 40× fewer training tokens than training from scratch.

The speedup depends on draft–target agreement. DistillSpec distils the draft toward the target using on-policy data and a task-tuned divergence, reporting 10–45% speedups over standard speculative decoding.
Switch Transformers distilled into dense models with about 1% of the parameters kept roughly 30% of the sparse teacher's quality gain.

Post-training, task-agnostic or task-specific expert pruning and dynamic expert skipping reduced mixture-of-experts model size and raised inference speed while keeping performance satisfactory on the tested tasks.

edges.relation: sub-1-bit compression of a trillion-parameter MoE
edges.text: QMoE compressed the 1.6-trillion-parameter SwitchTransformer-c2048 to under 160 GB, about 0.8 bits per parameter, with minor accuracy loss.
QLoRA backpropagates through a frozen 4-bit (NF4) base model into LoRA adapters, which made fine-tuning a 65B model on one 48 GB GPU possible.

edges.relation: parameters and compute as separate axes
edges.text: Routed models add parameters without adding FLOPs per token. Clark et al. fit scaling laws over both axes across five orders of magnitude and define an effective parameter count along which routed models scale.

Snell et al. compare spending FLOPs on a larger pretrained model with spending them on test-time search by a smaller one: test-time compute wins on easier and intermediate problems, pretraining on the hardest.
Best-of-N against a verifier is the baseline test-time strategy; allocating compute per prompt across search and revision was more than 4× more efficient.
Adding expected inference cost to the Chinchilla objective moves the optimum: with large inference demand, train a smaller model on more tokens.
Test-time scaling buys quality with per-query FLOPs, so whether it beats a larger model depends on query volume and latency budgets, not only on accuracy at matched FLOPs.
Cost per token falls with batch size while per-request latency rises; iteration-level scheduling moves the throughput–latency frontier rather than removing it.

Controlled decoding generalizes best-of-n: a learned prefix scorer reweights tokens or blocks, and blockwise best-of-K is one instance; both target a KL-regularized reward objective at inference time.
Best-of-n and beam search decode many continuations of one prompt; PagedAttention shares the prompt's KV blocks across them copy-on-write instead of duplicating them.
Training a low-bit student with a distillation loss from a full-precision teacher let quantized shallow students reach accuracy close to the full-precision teacher.

Exact under the stated rule: accept a drafted token x with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)) and, at the first rejection, sample from max(0, p − q) renormalized, with draft and target conditioned on the same prefix at the same temperature. Then every emitted token is distributed exactly as the target model's p, for any draft q. Floating-point differences and lenient-acceptance variants break exactness; the speedup, not the output distribution, depends on q.

edges.relation: soft-target cross-entropy is the log score
edges.text: Soft-target cross-entropy equals H(p_T) + KL(p_T‖q), the expected log score of the student q under the teacher's distribution p_T. Because the log score is strictly proper, for each input the unique minimizer is q = p_T. Exact when teacher and student use the same temperature and the student can represent p_T; otherwise training finds the KL projection onto the student family. Says nothing about inputs outside the transfer set.

edges.relation: growing exact state versus fixed recurrent state
edges.text: A KV cache keeps every past key and value, so decode memory grows linearly with context: a lossless but growing memory. A linear recurrent unit carries a fixed-size state, so per-token decode memory and time are constant in context length, at the price of a lossy summary of the past.

edges.relation: the cache collapses to a running sum
edges.text: For kernelized causal attention with feature map φ (not softmax), step t needs the cache only through S_t = Σ φ(k_i)v_iᵀ and z_t = Σ φ(k_i), so the growing KV cache can be replaced exactly by a fixed-size running sum. Exact for that attention form; it does not hold for softmax attention.

Proposed: evicting cache entries is a truncated-memory closure. Mori–Zwanzig reasoning says dropped history comes back as memory and noise terms. Test whether eviction policies lose the rare, decision-relevant history the thesis cares about, beyond what perplexity shows.

edges.relation: fixed-size state as a compressed belief
edges.text: Proposed: a trained recurrent state is a lossy candidate for the predictive (causal) state, the minimal statistic of the past that is sufficient for predicting the future. Whether a fixed-size LRU state approaches it on a process with known causal states is untested.

Processing a state cannot add Shannon information about the future (data processing inequality), but computation can raise usable information for a computationally bounded predictor (Xu et al.). Proposed reading: test-time compute extracts more from what the context or state retains; it cannot restore what was discarded. Untested for LLM test-time scaling.

Across the Pythia suite, LLC-based complexity estimates were closely, sometimes linearly, correlated with compressibility under quantization and factorization. A correlation across models, not a guarantee for a given model.

edges.relation: degenerate minima may tolerate coarse weights
edges.text: Proposed: quantization noise is a weight perturbation, so a minimum with a large low-loss volume (small learning coefficient) should tolerate it better. Flat-minimum description-length arguments predict this, but Hessian flatness can mislead for singular models; untested as a per-model predictor for LLMs.
Lloyd's k-means is the classical quantizer design; Deep Compression's trained quantization clusters each layer's weights with k-means and stores centroid indices plus a small codebook.

In Gao et al.'s synthetic setup, best-of-n against a proxy reward model first raises and then lowers the gold reward as n grows: a proxy–true divergence produced by selection alone, with no weight updates.
Conservative ensemble objectives (worst-case or uncertainty-weighted) practically eliminated overoptimization in best-of-n sampling in Coste et al.'s gold-model setup.

edges.relation: a training-free comparison point for RLHF
edges.text: Best-of-n is itself an aligned policy at a known cost: its KL from the reference policy is at most log n − (n−1)/n. Beirami et al. show this widely quoted formula is an upper bound, not an equality, and bound the win rate by n/(n+1).
Reasoning models are trained so that longer chains of thought raise accuracy, turning test-time compute into a learned capability; Snell et al. study how to allocate that compute per prompt.

edges.relation: the same samples serve two uses
edges.text: Sampling several answers supports majority voting (self-consistency) for accuracy and disagreement over meanings (semantic entropy) for confabulation detection; the samples are paid for once.
Grammar masking and scorer-guided decoding both change token choices without weight updates, and both move the output distribution away from the model's own conditional distribution.

Guardrails classify inputs and outputs from outside the model and block or escalate; inference-time interventions change the computation itself. Both act at deployment time and need monitoring for drift and evasion.

Proposed: inference-time interventions are the cheapest actuators for the thesis's correction interface, with no retraining and easy reversal and versioning. They count only if the effect persists through a session, unrelated capability holds on independent evaluations, and the intervention sits outside the model's write access.

The thesis's gap register asks whether correction machinery costs more than it helps. Proposed metric: energy or money per accepted, correctly corrected task at a fixed error rate, compared with the declared simple baselines.
Switch layers replace the transformer's dense feed-forward block with routed expert feed-forward blocks; attention is unchanged.

LoRA underperformed full fine-tuning on code and maths but better preserved performance outside the target domain, and full fine-tuning learned updates of 10–100× higher rank: evidence on how update structure affects retention.
Scaling laws give the bitter lesson a quantitative form within their tested ranges: loss falls predictably with compute, data and parameters for a fixed architecture family.
μP keeps optimal hyperparameters stable across width, so they can be tuned on a small proxy and transferred; scaling studies otherwise risk confusing model size with mistuning.

FlashAttention returns the same output as standard softmax attention: tiling with a running maximum and normalizer is an algebraic rearrangement of the same sums. Exact in real arithmetic; in floating point the results agree to rounding error because the summation order differs.

edges.relation: the course opens with these problem lists
edges.text: Week 1 asks what safe AI means and assigns the opening sections of Concrete Problems in AI Safety; week 4 assigns the introduction of Unsolved Problems in ML Safety.
The course separates model-specific from systemic safety issues and assigns a risk taxonomy, an essay arguing safety is not a model property, and a paper on hard choices in AI in its first week.
Two lectures cover reward functions and encoding human preferences, with readings on InstructGPT, reward-model overoptimization, open problems of RLHF and DPO.
The red-teaming lecture starts from adversarial examples in image classifiers and moves to adversarial attacks on aligned language models.
The last regular lecture asks how to supervise advanced AI, with debate, weak-to-strong generalization and measuring progress on scalable oversight among the readings.

edges.relation: reward hacking as a named open problem
edges.text: Avoiding reward hacking is one of the five problems in Concrete Problems, filed under having the wrong objective; the atlas's proxy-objectives topic gives the formal account of when proxy gains can reverse true ones.

edges.relation: scalable supervision as a named open problem
edges.text: Concrete Problems names scalable supervision, an objective too expensive to evaluate often, as an accident risk; later scalable-oversight work turns it into experiments with human and model overseers.
Safe exploration, avoiding catastrophic actions while still learning, is one of the five problems; constrained RL and safety filters are standard formal responses.
Unsolved Problems in ML Safety makes withstanding hazards, including adversarial and long-tail inputs, the first of its four research areas.
Hendrycks et al. already list reducing systemic hazards as a separate area; Narayanan and Kapoor push further, arguing many harms cannot be assessed at the model level at all.

edges.relation: the thesis's interfaces as answers to the classic problems
edges.text: Proposed mapping: objective uncertainty answers reward hacking and side effects, the correction interface answers scalable supervision, belief states address distributional shift, and the independent enforcer bounds unsafe exploration. Untested as a composition.
If harm depends on the deployment context, controls must sit in products, institutions and law; risk-tiered regulation and management frameworks are where those controls are specified.
The COMPAS case shows harm arising from how a risk score is used in sentencing, not only from the model; discrimination and exclusion head standard taxonomies of language-model risk.

edges.relation: AI feedback in place of human harm labels
edges.text: Constitutional AI keeps the RLHF pipeline but trains the harmlessness preference model on AI labels guided by written principles, and RLAIF matched RLHF on the tasks Lee et al. report.

edges.relation: using AI to help supervise AI
edges.text: Bai et al. motivate Constitutional AI as enlisting AI systems to help supervise other AIs, the core move of scalable oversight; human oversight is reduced to the list of principles.

edges.relation: whose principles go in the constitution
edges.text: The only human oversight in Constitutional AI is the list of principles, so the method concentrates the question of whose values count into who writes that list.

edges.relation: a single reward model aggregates disagreeing people
edges.text: Standard RLHF fits one reward to pooled annotators; Sorensen et al. report evidence that standard alignment procedures may reduce distributional pluralism in models.

edges.relation: one human in the model, many people in the world
edges.text: Assistance games model one human with a representable reward. Extending objective uncertainty to many stakeholders needs an aggregation or negotiation step, which Zhi-Xuan et al. argue preferences alone cannot supply. Proposed, not built.

edges.relation: a specified user versus many stakeholders
edges.text: The thesis defines aligned behaviour for a specified user within authorized constraints; pluralistic alignment asks who authorizes the constraints when users and affected people disagree. The thesis does not yet answer this.

edges.relation: what people want from AI varies by culture
edges.text: Ge et al. find that respondents from different cultural backgrounds weight control of and connection with AI differently, so a single notion of a good interaction already embeds a choice.
Guaranteed safe AI needs a verifier that certifies behaviour against a specification; sound neural-network verification is the existing technique, limited to input–output properties at modest scale.

edges.relation: certifying a safe set by reachability
edges.text: Reachability-based verifiers bound a network's outputs over an input set, the same object that invariance certificates for learned controllers need.

edges.relation: certified robustness within a perturbation set
edges.text: Local robustness, no misclassification anywhere in a small ball around an input, is the standard property neural-network verifiers prove and the one adversarial examples violate.

edges.relation: testing finds failures, verification proves absence
edges.text: Red teaming and adversarial search can only exhibit failures; sound verification proves their absence, but only for a formal property over a bounded input set.
In Birhane et al.'s audit, growing the dataset from LAION-400M to LAION-2B increased hateful content and made trained models label Black men's faces as criminal roughly two to five times as often.

edges.relation: more data is not cleaner data
edges.text: Scaling laws predict falling loss with more data; the hate-scaling audit shows that the same scaling of web data can increase harmful content and downstream bias.

edges.relation: poisoning as the way backdoors get in
edges.text: Carlini et al. show that poisoning 0.01% of LAION-400M or COYO-700M would have cost about $60; sleeper-agent results show that behaviour inserted this way can survive safety training.

In O'Brien et al.'s 6.9B-parameter models, filtering dual-use text out before pretraining held up against adversarial fine-tuning more than an order of magnitude longer than safeguards added in post-training.

edges.relation: unlearning as a correction that must persist
